name: Barbell Bench Press
secondary: Anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, serratus anterior
equipment: Barbell, flat bench, power rack with safeties
steps: Lie supine with eyes directly under the bar; plant feet flat and drive them into the floor.
Retract and depress the scapulae, creating a small natural arch in the lower back.
Grip the bar so forearms are vertical at the bottom position — usually 1.5x shoulder width.
Unrack, bring the bar to the lower chest/sternum with elbows at roughly 45-60 degrees from the torso.
Touch the chest under control, then drive the bar up and slightly back toward the shoulders.
breathing: Inhale and brace at the top, hold through the descent, exhale forcefully past the sticking point.
mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the ribcage to generate momentum.
Flaring elbows to 90 degrees, which shears the shoulder joint.
Letting the hips lift off the bench to shorten the range of motion.
Gripping the bar so wide that forearms angle inward at the bottom.
tips: Think of pushing yourself away from the bar rather than pushing the bar away.
Screw the feet into the floor to build whole-body tension before the first rep.
Wrists stack directly over the elbows throughout the press.
safety: Always use a spotter or set safety pins at chest height.
Never use a thumbless (suicide) grip.
Warm up the rotator cuff before heavy loads.
avoid: Acute shoulder impingement or labral pain
progression: Add 2.5 kg per week; introduce 2-second paused reps at the chest.
regression: Dumbbell bench press, machine chest press, or elevated push-up.

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
steps: Set the bench to 30-45 degrees. Steeper angles shift work to the front delt.
Set the shoulder blades back and down against the pad; feet flat on the floor.
Unrack and lower the bar toward the upper chest, just below the collarbone.
Keep elbows tucked to about 45 degrees from the torso.
Press up and slightly back until the elbows are near lockout.
breathing: Inhale on the descent; exhale as the bar clears the halfway point.
mistakes: Setting the bench above 45 degrees and turning it into a shoulder press.
Touching the bar too high on the throat line.
Losing scapular retraction as fatigue accumulates.
tips: 30 degrees gives the best clavicular recruitment for most builds.
Keep the bar path slightly diagonal, not straight up and down.
Pause 1 second at the chest to eliminate bounce.
safety: Use a spotter for the last two reps of a hard set.
Do not shrug the shoulders toward the ears under load.
progression: Progress load, then add a paused variant; finish with incline dumbbell press.
regression: Incline dumbbell press or incline machine press.

name: Decline Barbell Bench Press
steps: Secure the legs in the roller pads and lie back on a 15-30 degree decline.
Have a spotter hand off the bar — self-unracking on a decline is awkward.
Lower the bar to the lower chest, just above the sternum's base.
Keep elbows moderately tucked; press straight up over the lower chest.
breathing: Inhale at the top, exhale through the concentric.
mistakes: Unracking without a spotter.
Letting the head hang and creating pressure in the skull.
Excessive decline angle beyond 30 degrees.
tips: Decline reduces anterior deltoid demand — useful when the shoulders are cranky.
Keep range of motion full; the decline already shortens it slightly.
safety: Always use a spotter for the hand-off and re-rack.
Sit up slowly afterwards to avoid a blood-pressure drop.
progression: Add load, then progress to weighted chest dips.
regression: Chest dip or flat dumbbell press.

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
secondary: Anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, rotator cuff
steps: Sit on the bench with the dumbbells resting on the thighs.
Kick the dumbbells up one knee at a time as you lie back.
Set the dumbbells at chest level, palms facing forward, elbows at 45 degrees.
Press up and slightly together without clanging the bells.
Lower under control until the elbows are just below torso level.
breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
mistakes: Lowering the weights past a comfortable stretch and straining the shoulder capsule.
Pressing the dumbbells straight up with no convergence.
Dropping the dumbbells from the top instead of returning them to the thighs.
tips: Dumbbells allow a longer range and a more shoulder-friendly path than a barbell.
Independent limbs expose and correct side-to-side strength asymmetry.
Squeeze the handles hard — grip tension improves pressing stability.
safety: Learn the safe kick-up and set-down technique before going heavy.
Never let a training partner pull on your wrists to assist.
progression: Increase load; then progress to a 3-second eccentric.
regression: Floor press (shortened range) or machine chest press.

name: Incline Dumbbell Press
steps: Set the bench to 30 degrees and sit with dumbbells on the thighs.
Kick up and lie back, keeping the shoulder blades pinned to the pad.
Start with the dumbbells at upper-chest height, elbows under the wrists.
Press up and inward, stopping just short of the bells touching.
Lower slowly until a mild stretch is felt across the upper chest.
mistakes: Bench angle too steep, converting it into a shoulder press.
Bouncing the dumbbells off the chest.
Letting the elbows drift behind the torso at the bottom.
tips: Keep a slight bend in the elbows at lockout to keep tension on the chest.
A neutral (palms-in) grip is a good option for irritated shoulders.
safety: Set the dumbbells down on the thighs, not the floor beside you.
Do not arch aggressively on an incline.
progression: Add load, then unilateral alternating presses for core demand.
regression: Incline machine press or incline push-up.

name: Flat Dumbbell Fly
steps: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand, pressed above the chest, palms facing each other.
Set a fixed, soft bend of about 15 degrees in the elbows and keep it there.
Open the arms in a wide arc until a stretch is felt across the chest.
Stop when the upper arms reach torso level — do not go deeper.
Hug the arms back together along the same arc, squeezing the chest at the top.
breathing: Inhale as the arms open, exhale as they close.
mistakes: Using a bent-arm press instead of a true arc.
Going far too heavy — the fly is a stretch-position movement, not a strength lift.
Dropping the arms below bench level and overloading the shoulder capsule.
tips: The elbow angle is fixed. If it changes, the load is too heavy.
Slow the eccentric; this movement earns most of its stimulus in the stretch.
Finish the rep by imagining you are squeezing a ball between the forearms.
safety: Start with 30-40% of your dumbbell press load.
Never bounce out of the bottom stretch.
progression: Add a 2-second hold in the stretched position; then move to cable flys for constant tension.
regression: Pec deck machine — fixed path, easier to control.

name: Incline Dumbbell Fly
steps: Set the bench to 30 degrees; hold dumbbells above the upper chest, palms facing.
Lock a soft elbow bend and open the arms in a wide arc.
Stop at torso level where the upper chest stretch peaks.
Return along the identical arc and squeeze.
mistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows (turning it into a press).
Excessive range that stresses the front of the shoulder.
tips: Lighter than the flat fly — the incline lengthens the lever.
Pause at the top for a full second to raise time under tension.
safety: Use a spotter's knee under the elbows if you are new to the movement.
progression: Progress to incline cable fly.
regression: Pec deck or a lighter flat fly.

name: Cable Crossover (High to Low)
steps: Set both pulleys above head height and take a handle in each hand.
Step forward into a split stance so the cables are under light tension.
Hinge the torso forward about 15 degrees; soft bend in the elbows.
Sweep the hands down and together toward the belt line, crossing slightly.
Squeeze for one second, then let the cables draw the arms back with control.
breathing: Exhale as the hands come together, inhale on the return.
mistakes: Standing bolt upright, which turns the movement into a triceps pushdown.
Using so much weight that the torso rocks forward to finish the rep.
Letting the elbows straighten and lock.
tips: Cables keep tension constant across the entire arc — unlike dumbbells.
Cross the hands slightly to add adduction and hit the inner chest.
This is the highest-value finishing movement for lower chest.
safety: Control the return; a snapped-back cable can wrench the shoulder.
progression: Progress to a 2-second squeeze plus a slow 4-second eccentric.
regression: Pec deck machine or resistance band fly.

name: Cable Crossover (Low to High)
steps: Set both pulleys at the lowest setting; grab a handle in each hand, palms forward.
Step into a staggered stance, chest tall, slight forward lean.
Sweep the hands up and inward, finishing at collarbone height.
Squeeze, then lower along the same arc under control.
breathing: Exhale on the sweep up, inhale on the return.
mistakes: Shrugging the traps to help lift the handles.
Finishing above the head, which hands the work to the front delt.
tips: Stop the hands at chin height — beyond that the chest disengages.
Keep the ribcage down; do not lean back.
safety: Keep the wrists neutral, not extended.
progression: Single-arm version for greater range and core anti-rotation demand.
regression: Incline dumbbell fly.

name: Pec Deck Machine
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles sit at mid-chest height.
Sit tall with the back flat against the pad and feet planted.
Grip the handles with a soft elbow bend and shoulder blades pinned back.
Bring the handles together in front of the sternum and squeeze for one second.
Open slowly until a stretch is felt, stopping before the shoulders roll forward.
mistakes: Setting the seat too low, forcing the elbows above the shoulders.
Letting the shoulders round forward at the stretch.
Slamming the pads together.
tips: The safest chest isolation for beginners — the path is fixed.
Excellent choice as a pre-exhaust before pressing.
Drive the elbows together, not the hands.
safety: Set the range-of-motion pin so the stretch never becomes painful.
progression: Add a 3-second eccentric or a drop set on the final round.
regression: Resistance band fly, seated.

name: Machine Chest Press
steps: Set the seat so the handles align with the mid-chest, not the collarbone.
Sit with the back flat, feet planted, shoulder blades against the pad.
Press the handles forward until the elbows are nearly straight.
Return under control until the hands are level with the chest.
mistakes: Seat too high, which shifts load onto the shoulders.
Locking the elbows aggressively at the end range.
Letting the weight stack touch down between reps.
tips: The best entry point for a beginner learning the horizontal press pattern.
Also the safest way to train to true muscular failure without a spotter.
safety: Keep one hand able to release if a set fails.
progression: Move to dumbbell bench press once the pattern is stable.
regression: Resistance band chest press.

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
steps: Position the bench so the bar path descends over the mid-chest.
Set the shoulder blades back; grip slightly wider than shoulders.
Rotate the bar to unhook it, lower to the chest, press back up.
Rotate to re-hook at the top of the final rep.
mistakes: Placing the bench too far forward so the bar lands on the throat.
Relying on the fixed path and never developing free-weight stability.
tips: Useful for training close to failure alone, since the safety hooks catch the bar.
Set the safety stops just below chest level before the first rep.
safety: Verify the hook mechanism engages before unloading the bar.
Never train to failure without the safeties set.
avoid: Shoulder impingement (fixed path may not suit your anatomy)
progression: Transition to barbell bench press for stabiliser development.
regression: Machine chest press.

name: Standard Push-Up
secondary: Triceps brachii, anterior deltoid, rectus abdominis, serratus anterior
steps: Place hands slightly wider than the shoulders, directly under the collarbones.
Extend the legs, squeeze the glutes and brace the abdominals into a rigid plank.
Lower the chest toward the floor, elbows tracking back at roughly 45 degrees.
Stop when the chest is a fist's height from the ground.
Press the floor away, pushing the upper back apart at the top.
breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag, which loads the lumbar spine.
Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees and grinding the shoulder.
Dropping the head forward so the chin leads instead of the chest.
Half-repping — stopping high because of fatigue.
tips: The push-up is a moving plank. If the core fails, the set is over.
Push the ground away rather than pulling yourself up.
Protract the shoulder blades fully at the top to train the serratus.
safety: Keep the wrists warm; use push-up handles or fists if wrist extension hurts.
progression: Elevate the feet, add a weight vest, or progress to archer push-ups.
regression: Incline push-up with hands on a bench or wall.

name: Incline Push-Up
steps: Place the hands on a raised surface, slightly wider than shoulder width.
Walk the feet back until the body is a straight line from head to heels.
Lower the chest to the surface with the elbows at 45 degrees.
Press back up and fully extend.
mistakes: Placing the hands too far forward and stressing the shoulders.
Piking the hips upward.
Using a wobbly or rolling surface.
tips: The higher the surface, the easier the rep. Lower it gradually week by week.
This is the single best regression for a first push-up.
A kitchen counter, staircase, or park bench all work.
safety: Ensure the surface cannot slide.
progression: Lower the surface every 1-2 weeks until you reach the floor.
regression: Wall push-up — the easiest variation available.

name: Decline Push-Up
steps: Place the feet on a bench or box roughly 30-45 cm high.
Set the hands on the floor slightly wider than the shoulders.
Brace hard — the elevated feet increase the anti-extension demand.
Lower the chest to the floor, then press back to full extension.
mistakes: Elevating the feet so high it becomes a shoulder press.
Letting the lower back arch as the core fatigues.
tips: Feet elevation shifts load to the upper chest and front delt.
Stop the set the moment the hips sag — quality over count.
safety: Do not use an unstable box.
Keep the neck neutral; do not crane the head.
progression: Elevate the feet higher, or add a weight vest.
regression: Standard push-up on the floor.

name: Diamond Push-Up
steps: Form a diamond with the thumbs and index fingers directly under the sternum.
Set a rigid plank; squeeze the glutes.
Lower the chest toward the hands, keeping the elbows tucked close to the ribs.
Press up until the elbows lock without letting the hips rise first.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows outward, which defeats the triceps emphasis.
Placing the hands too far forward, straining the wrists.
Shortening the range because the leverage is harder.
tips: This is the highest-triceps-activation bodyweight push in most EMG studies.
If the wrists complain, do it on parallel handles or fists.
safety: Warm the wrists thoroughly.
Do not force the hands into a perfect diamond if it hurts.
progression: Elevate the feet, then add a weight vest.
regression: Close-grip push-up with hands shoulder-width apart.

name: Wide-Grip Push-Up
steps: Place the hands roughly 1.5x shoulder width apart, fingers slightly turned out.
Brace the trunk and squeeze the glutes.
Lower until the upper arms reach torso level.
Press up while imagining you are pulling the hands toward each other.
mistakes: Going so wide the shoulders take the load instead of the chest.
Sagging hips.
Bottoming out with the chest on the floor and resting.
tips: Wider hands increase the chest stretch but reduce total range.
Turn the fingers out 15-20 degrees to spare the wrists.
safety: Stop if you feel a pinch at the front of the shoulder.
progression: Elevate the feet or add a pause at the bottom.
regression: Standard-width or incline push-up.

name: Archer Push-Up
steps: Take a wide push-up position, hands well outside shoulder width.
Shift the bodyweight toward the right hand as you lower.
The left arm straightens out to the side, acting as a kickstand.
Press back up through the working arm, then alternate sides.
mistakes: Letting the straight arm bend and share the load.
Rotating the hips instead of keeping the pelvis square.
Rushing before the standard push-up is strong.
tips: A genuine bridge toward the one-arm push-up.
Keep the extended arm's palm rotated so the fingers point sideways.
safety: Master 20 clean standard push-ups first.
progression: Reduce the assist from the straight arm; then attempt one-arm negatives.
regression: Standard push-up, or archer push-up with knees down.

name: Deficit Push-Up
equipment: Two low boxes, books, or push-up handles
steps: Set two low, stable surfaces slightly wider than the shoulders.
Take a push-up position with the hands on the surfaces.
Lower until the chest drops below the level of the hands.
Press back to full lockout without losing the plank.
mistakes: Sinking so deep the shoulders round forward under load.
Using surfaces that can shift or roll.
tips: The extra range increases the stretch and the hypertrophy stimulus.
Push-up handles also keep the wrists neutral.
safety: Test the surfaces with bodyweight before performing a set.
progression: Increase deficit height, or elevate the feet as well.
regression: Standard floor push-up.

name: Ring / TRX Push-Up
secondary: Serratus anterior, rotator cuff, core, triceps brachii
equipment: Gymnastic rings or TRX suspension trainer
steps: Set the rings or straps at roughly knee to mid-shin height.
Take a plank position with the handles under the shoulders, arms straight.
Externally rotate the hands so the thumbs point slightly outward.
Lower the chest between the handles, elbows at 45 degrees.
Press up and turn the hands out again at the top.
mistakes: Letting the handles drift wide and wobble uncontrolled.
Attempting rings before floor push-ups are strong.
Losing the plank and piking at the hips.
tips: Instability roughly doubles rotator cuff and serratus demand.
Raise the handles to reduce difficulty; lower them to increase it.
The turn-out at the top adds a valuable external-rotation cue.
safety: Check the anchor point rating before every session.
Keep the straps short enough that the handles cannot swing away.
progression: Lower the anchor, elevate the feet, or add a weight vest.
regression: Raise the handles higher for a steeper, easier angle.

name: Chest Dip
steps: Mount the bars with arms locked and shoulders pressed down away from the ears.
Lean the torso forward roughly 30 degrees and cross the ankles behind.
Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor, elbows flared slightly.
Press back up while maintaining the forward lean throughout.
breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the press.
mistakes: Staying upright, which turns it into a triceps dip.
Descending below parallel and overstretching the shoulder capsule.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the bottom.
Bouncing out of the bottom position.
tips: Forward lean is the switch that moves load from triceps to chest.
Depress the scapulae hard at the top of every rep.
Stop at parallel — deeper is not better here.
safety: Build with band-assisted or machine-assisted dips first.
Never bounce; the bottom of a dip is the shoulder's most vulnerable position.
progression: Add a dip belt with 5-10 kg; then progress to weighted ring dips.
regression: Band-assisted dip, or bench dip with feet on the floor.

name: Svend Press
equipment: Two light weight plates (2.5-5 kg each)
steps: Stand tall and press two plates together flat between the palms at chest height.
Squeeze the plates hard enough that they do not slip — that squeeze is the exercise.
Press the plates straight forward until the arms are extended.
Return to the chest, maintaining maximum inward pressure the whole time.
mistakes: Letting the squeeze relax during the press.
Using plates so heavy the wrists collapse.
Shrugging the shoulders.
tips: Pure isometric adduction — excellent as a chest pre-exhaust or finisher.
Cannot be loaded heavy, and does not need to be.
safety: Perform over a mat; a dropped plate on bare feet is a genuine risk.
progression: Hold the end position for 5 seconds on the final rep.
regression: Squeeze a foam roller or ball between the palms.

name: Landmine Press
equipment: Barbell in a landmine attachment or corner
steps: Wedge one end of a barbell in a landmine sleeve or a padded corner.
Kneel or stand in a staggered stance, holding the free end at the shoulder.
Brace the trunk and press the bar up and forward along its natural arc.
Lock out with the arm extended, then return to the shoulder under control.
mistakes: Fighting the arc and trying to press straight up.
Letting the ribcage flare and the lower back extend.
Rotating the torso to gain leverage.
tips: The arced path is far friendlier to shoulders than an overhead press.
An excellent primary press for anyone with impingement history.
The half-kneeling version doubles as an anti-extension core drill.
safety: Anchor the bar end so it cannot slide out.
Start with the bar alone before loading plates.
progression: Move from half-kneeling to standing; then load with plates.
regression: Incline dumbbell press at a low angle.

name: Dumbbell Floor Press
steps: Lie on the floor with knees bent, feet flat, dumbbells at the chest.
Press up until the arms are nearly straight, shoulder blades still on the floor.
Lower until the back of the upper arms just touch the floor.
Pause briefly on the floor, then press again — no bounce.
mistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor.
Arching the lower back hard to generate leverage.
Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees.
tips: The floor caps the range, protecting an irritated shoulder.
Also the best home press when no bench is available.
Great tool for building lockout strength.
safety: Rest the dumbbells on the hips and roll back to get into position safely.
progression: Add load, then move to a full-range bench press.
regression: Machine chest press or push-up.

name: Resistance Band Chest Press
equipment: Long loop resistance band, anchor point
steps: Anchor a band behind you at chest height (door anchor or sturdy post).
Face away, hold a handle in each hand at chest level, step forward for tension.
Adopt a staggered stance and brace the core.
Press the hands forward and slightly together until the arms extend.
Return slowly, resisting the band's pull.
mistakes: Standing square, which lets the band pull you backwards.
Letting the band snap the hands back at speed.
Anchoring to a door that opens toward you.
tips: Bands give ascending resistance — hardest at lockout, matching the strength curve.
The single most travel-friendly chest builder available.
Step further forward to increase tension without buying a heavier band.
safety: Inspect the band for nicks or tears before every session.
Never anchor at eye level in a way that can recoil into the face.
progression: Use a thicker band or step further from the anchor.
regression: Machine chest press or incline push-up.

name: Resistance Band Fly
steps: Anchor the band behind you at chest height.
Hold a handle in each hand, arms out wide, soft bend in the elbows.
Step forward until the band is taut with the arms open.
Bring the hands together in front of the sternum in a wide arc; squeeze.
Open slowly back to the stretch.
mistakes: Bending the elbows into a press.
Allowing the band to yank the arms back open.
tips: Bands hold tension at the fully contracted position, which dumbbells cannot.
Pairs perfectly with band chest press as a two-move home chest session.
safety: Check the anchor and the band for wear.
progression: Thicker band, or a longer step forward.
regression: Pec deck machine, or a seated band fly.

name: Clap Push-Up
steps: Start in a rigid push-up position with the core braced hard.
Descend to a normal push-up depth, then explode upward as violently as possible.
Leave the floor, clap the hands once, and return them under the shoulders.
Absorb the landing by immediately bending the elbows into the next rep.
breathing: Exhale sharply on the push, inhale on the reset.
mistakes: Attempting these before 25 strict push-ups are easy.
Landing with locked, straight elbows — a common wrist and elbow injury cause.
Continuing when the reps lose height, which trains slowness, not power.
tips: Stop the set the moment hand height drops. Power work is not endurance work.
Land soft. The landing is the exercise, not the clap.
Keep total reps low: 3-5 per set is plenty.
safety: Perform on a mat or grass, never on tile.
Warm up the wrists and shoulders fully.
progression: Progress to double-clap or behind-the-back clap push-ups.
regression: Explosive push-up without leaving the floor, or hands-elevated clap push-up.

name: Dumbbell Pullover
steps: Lie along or across a flat bench with the hips slightly lower than the shoulders.
Hold one dumbbell with both palms cupped under the top plate.
Start with the arms extended above the chest, elbows softly bent.
Lower the dumbbell back over the head until a deep chest and lat stretch is felt.
Pull it back over the chest along the same arc.
breathing: Inhale as the weight travels overhead, exhale as it returns.
mistakes: Going too heavy and losing control behind the head.
Bending the elbows to cheat the weight up.
Overextending the lumbar spine at the stretch.
tips: Keep the ribcage pulled down; the stretch should be felt in the chest, not the back.
A rare movement that loads both the chest and lat in the lengthened position.
Use a lighter weight than instinct suggests.
safety: Have a spotter or use a lighter dumbbell if performed across the bench.
Ensure the dumbbell's collars are tight.
progression: Add load slowly; or switch to a cable pullover for constant tension.
regression: Straight-arm cable pulldown.

name: Medicine Ball Chest Pass (Wall)
steps: Stand 1.5-2 m from a solid wall, ball held at chest height.
Set an athletic stance: knees soft, chest tall, core braced.
Push the ball explosively at the wall, extending both arms fully.
Catch the rebound with soft elbows and immediately reset for the next throw.
breathing: Exhale sharply on the throw, inhale on the catch.
mistakes: Throwing with the arms only and no leg drive.
Catching with straight, locked arms.
Using a bouncy ball that returns unpredictably.
tips: Trains the rate of force development the bench press cannot.
Keep reps at 5-8 and rest fully — this is a power drill.
Use a non-bouncing slam-style ball if the rebound is unmanageable.
safety: Use a concrete or brick wall, never drywall or glass.
Clear the area behind you.
progression: Heavier ball, or single-arm passes.
regression: Standing band chest press performed quickly.

name: Conventional Deadlift
secondary: Hamstrings, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, forearm flexors
steps: Stand with mid-foot under the bar, feet hip-width. The bar touches the shins.
Hinge at the hips and grip just outside the knees; drop the hips until the shins meet the bar.
Set the chest tall, lats squeezed (imagine crushing oranges in the armpits), spine neutral.
Take the slack out of the bar, brace, then push the floor away and stand up.
Lock out by driving the hips forward — do not lean back at the top.
breathing: Big brace and hold through the pull; exhale at lockout or between reps.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back — the single most common cause of deadlift injury.
Yanking the bar off the floor without taking out the slack.
Hyperextending the spine at lockout.
tips: The deadlift is a push, not a pull. Drive the floor down.
Keep the bar in contact with the legs the whole way up.
If the hips shoot up first, the weight is too heavy.
safety: Master the hip hinge pattern with a dowel before loading.
Never round the spine to complete a rep — reset instead.
avoid: Acute lower back pain or disc herniation
progression: Add 2.5-5 kg per session while form holds; then add deficit deadlifts.
regression: Trap bar deadlift or Romanian deadlift from the knee.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
steps: Step inside the hex bar with feet hip-width.
Hinge and grip the neutral handles; hips slightly lower than a straight-bar setup.
Brace, chest tall, then stand by driving the feet into the floor.
Lower under control until the plates touch, then reset.
breathing: Brace at the bottom, exhale at the top.
mistakes: Squatting the weight up with the hips too low.
Rounding the upper back.
Bouncing plates off the floor.
tips: The neutral grip and centred load make this far safer to learn than a straight bar.
The best first heavy hinge for most ZITLAS users.
safety: Use the high handles until hip mobility allows the low handles.
Keep the neck neutral.
progression: Progress load, then move to a conventional barbell deadlift.
regression: Kettlebell deadlift or dumbbell Romanian deadlift.

name: Romanian Deadlift
steps: Stand tall holding the bar at the hips, knees softly bent (about 15 degrees).
Push the hips backwards, letting the bar slide down the thighs.
Keep the shins vertical and the spine neutral; descend until a hamstring stretch limits you.
Drive the hips forward to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.
breathing: Inhale on the way down, exhale standing up.
mistakes: Bending the knees more as the bar descends — that makes it a deadlift.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs.
Chasing depth by rounding the lower back.
tips: Depth is set by hamstring flexibility, not by touching the floor.
Keep the lats engaged so the bar stays glued to the thigh.
safety: Start with an empty bar or light dumbbells.
Stop the set if the back rounds.
progression: Add load; then progress to single-leg Romanian deadlifts.
regression: Dumbbell RDL from a shortened range, or a hip hinge with a dowel.

name: Pull-Up (Pronated Grip)
secondary: Biceps brachii, teres major, rhomboids, lower trapezius
steps: Hang from the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than the shoulders.
Begin by depressing the shoulder blades — pull them down before the elbows bend.
Drive the elbows down and back until the chin clears the bar.
Lower under full control to a complete dead hang.
breathing: Exhale on the way up, inhale on the descent.
mistakes: Kipping or swinging the legs to generate momentum.
Stopping short of a full hang, which sacrifices the strongest range.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the bottom.
tips: Initiate with the scapulae, not the arms. This one cue fixes most pull-ups.
Squeeze the glutes and brace to stop the body swinging.
safety: Build with negatives and band-assisted reps before attempting full reps.
Do not add load until 8 clean bodyweight reps are possible.
progression: Add a dip belt with 2.5-5 kg; then progress to weighted or archer pull-ups.
regression: Band-assisted pull-up, lat pulldown, or inverted row.

name: Chin-Up (Supinated Grip)
steps: Hang with an underhand grip at roughly shoulder width.
Depress the shoulder blades, then pull the chest toward the bar.
Clear the chin above the bar and squeeze at the top.
Lower slowly to a full hang.
mistakes: Swinging or kipping.
Cutting the descent short.
Flaring the elbows wide, which reduces biceps leverage.
tips: The supinated grip recruits far more biceps — most people can do more chin-ups than pull-ups.
An excellent first vertical pull for beginners.
safety: Keep the wrists stacked; if the elbows ache, switch to a neutral grip.
progression: Add load, or slow the eccentric to 5 seconds.
regression: Band-assisted chin-up or inverted row.

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
steps: Grip two parallel handles, palms facing each other.
Depress the scapulae, then pull the sternum toward the handles.
Clear the chin, squeeze, and lower under control.
mistakes: Kipping.
Partial range at the bottom.
Craning the neck to clear the bar.
tips: The most shoulder- and elbow-friendly vertical pull.
The default choice for anyone with cranky elbows.
safety: Check the handle attachment is secure.
progression: Add a weight vest.
regression: Band-assisted neutral pull-up.

name: Lat Pulldown (Wide Grip)
steps: Set the thigh pad so it pins the legs firmly.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder width; sit tall with a slight backward lean.
Pull the bar to the upper chest by driving the elbows down and back.
Squeeze the lats for one second, then let the bar rise until the arms fully extend.
breathing: Exhale pulling down, inhale on the return.
mistakes: Pulling the bar behind the neck — high risk, no added benefit.
Leaning far back and turning it into a row.
Using the biceps to yank instead of driving with the elbows.
tips: Let the shoulder blades rise fully at the top — that stretch is the point.
Think of the hands as hooks. The lats do the work.
The best regression on the path to a first pull-up.
safety: Never pull behind the neck.
Do not let the stack pull you off the seat.
progression: Reduce assistance until bodyweight pull-ups become possible.
regression: Band-assisted lat pulldown, or a seated band pulldown.

name: Close-Grip Lat Pulldown
steps: Attach a V-bar and set the thigh pad.
Sit tall, grip the neutral handles, lean back about 15 degrees.
Pull the handles to the sternum, elbows driving straight down.
Control the return to a full stretch.
mistakes: Excessive backward lean.
Bouncing the stack at the bottom of the stretch.
tips: The close neutral grip emphasises the lower lat fibres and lets you load heavier.
Keep the chest up and the elbows tracking past the ribs.
safety: Keep the thigh pad tight to stop the hips lifting.
progression: Increase load, or add a 3-second squeeze at the bottom.
regression: Seated cable row.

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
secondary: Trapezius, posterior deltoid, erector spinae, biceps brachii
steps: Stand hip-width, hinge until the torso is 15-45 degrees above horizontal.
Grip the bar just outside the knees, spine neutral, shins vertical.
Row the bar to the lower ribs or upper abdomen, elbows tracking back.
Lower under control to full arm extension without letting the torso rise.
breathing: Inhale and brace before the rep; exhale at the top of the row.
mistakes: Using the torso as a lever and jerking the bar up.
Rounding the lumbar spine.
Rowing to the chest with flared elbows, which turns it into a rear delt row.
tips: Set the torso angle and do not let it change for the whole set.
Pull with the elbows; the hands are hooks.
If the last reps require body English, the set is finished.
safety: Brace the trunk hard throughout.
Do not perform with an acutely painful back.
progression: Add load; then progress to a Pendlay row from a dead stop.
regression: Chest-supported row or single-arm dumbbell row.

name: Pendlay Row
steps: Hinge until the torso is parallel to the floor; the bar rests on the ground.
Grip just outside the knees, brace, and explosively row the bar to the lower sternum.
Return the bar all the way to the floor and let it settle for a beat.
Reset the brace before every rep.
breathing: Inhale and brace on the floor, exhale at the top.
mistakes: Letting the torso rise above parallel.
Bouncing the bar off the floor to gain momentum.
Rounding the back to reach the bar.
tips: Every rep starts from a dead stop, removing the stretch reflex.
Builds explosive pulling strength for deadlifts and Olympic lifts.
Keep sets short — 5 hard reps is the sweet spot.
safety: Requires strong isometric back endurance. Master the bent-over row first.
progression: Add load, keeping the torso strictly parallel.
regression: Standard bent-over row with a higher torso angle.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
secondary: Rhomboids, posterior deltoid, biceps brachii, obliques
steps: Place the left knee and left hand on a bench, right foot on the floor.
Let the right arm hang, dumbbell in hand, spine flat and parallel to the floor.
Row the dumbbell to the hip, driving the elbow past the ribs.
Lower under control until the lat is fully stretched, then repeat.
mistakes: Rotating the torso to hoist the weight.
Rowing straight up to the shoulder rather than back to the hip.
Shrugging at the top.
tips: Keep the hips square. If the torso twists, drop the weight.
The supported position removes lower back fatigue, so you can push the lats harder.
Allow the shoulder blade to travel — protract at the bottom, retract at the top.
safety: Ensure the bench is stable.
Keep a neutral neck, eyes down.
progression: Add load, or perform a 2-second pause at the top.
regression: Chest-supported dumbbell row.

name: Chest-Supported Row
secondary: Middle trapezius, posterior deltoid, biceps brachii
steps: Set an incline bench to 30-45 degrees and lie chest-down on it.
Let the arms hang straight, dumbbell in each hand.
Row both dumbbells toward the hips, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Lower slowly to a full stretch.
mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad to cheat.
Shrugging instead of retracting.
Cutting the stretch short.
tips: Chest support eliminates the lower back as a limiting factor.
The best rowing choice for anyone with back pain history.
Pause 1 second with the shoulder blades pinned.
safety: Adjust the bench height so the dumbbells clear the floor.
progression: Add load; then progress to a T-bar or barbell row.
regression: Seated cable row.

name: Seated Cable Row
secondary: Middle trapezius, biceps brachii, posterior deltoid
steps: Sit with a slight knee bend, feet on the platform, chest tall.
Grip the handle, arms extended, and let the shoulder blades protract forward.
Row the handle to the navel, driving the elbows straight back.
Squeeze for one second, then return slowly to a full stretch.
breathing: Exhale rowing, inhale on the return.
mistakes: Rocking the torso back and forth like a rowing machine.
Rounding the lower back at the stretch.
Pulling the handle to the chest instead of the navel.
tips: Let the shoulder blades move — a locked scapula wastes half the exercise.
The torso stays roughly vertical throughout.
safety: Do not let the stack yank you forward at the end of a hard set.
avoid: Acute lower back pain (use a chest-supported row instead)
progression: Increase load, or add a 2-second squeeze.
regression: Resistance band seated row.

name: Inverted Row
equipment: Barbell in a rack, Smith machine, or TRX
steps: Set a bar at hip height and lie underneath it.
Grip slightly wider than shoulders; body straight from head to heels.
Pull the chest to the bar, squeezing the shoulder blades.
Lower under control to full arm extension.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Shrugging the shoulders instead of retracting.
Cutting the range short and never touching the bar.
tips: Raise the bar to make it easier; lower it (or elevate the feet) to make it harder.
The most scalable horizontal pull in existence — usable by a 10-year-old or an athlete.
The best partner exercise for building a first pull-up.
safety: Confirm the bar is locked into the rack pins.
progression: Lower the bar, elevate the feet, then add a weight vest.
regression: Raise the bar higher for a steeper, easier angle.

name: T-Bar Row
secondary: Middle trapezius, posterior deltoid, erector spinae
equipment: T-bar row machine or landmine + V-handle
steps: Straddle the bar, hinge to a 30-45 degree torso angle, knees soft.
Grip the handles and set a neutral spine with the chest tall.
Row the handle to the lower sternum, elbows close to the body.
Lower slowly to full extension.
mistakes: Standing up as the set fatigues.
Rounding the lower back.
Using momentum from a hip thrust.
tips: The neutral grip and centred load allow heavy loading with less lumbar shear than a barbell row.
A chest-supported T-bar removes the back entirely if that is a concern.
safety: Anchor the bar end securely if using a landmine setup.
progression: Add load, or move to a chest-supported T-bar for stricter form.
regression: Chest-supported dumbbell row.

name: Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown
secondary: Teres major, triceps long head, rectus abdominis
equipment: Cable machine, straight bar or rope, high pulley
steps: Stand facing a high pulley, feet hip-width, hinge slightly at the hips.
Hold the bar with straight arms, a soft elbow bend locked in place.
Sweep the bar down in an arc until it reaches the thighs.
Let the arms rise back overhead until a lat stretch is felt.
breathing: Exhale on the sweep down, inhale on the return.
mistakes: Bending the elbows and turning it into a triceps pushdown.
Standing bolt upright, which shortens the arc.
Using so much weight that the torso rocks.
tips: The only reliable way to train the lat without the biceps being a limiting factor.
Superb as a lat pre-exhaust or a pump finisher.
safety: Keep the ribcage down; do not extend the lumbar spine.
progression: Add a 2-second squeeze at the thighs, or use a single-arm variant.
regression: Resistance band straight-arm pulldown.

name: Face Pull
equipment: Cable machine, rope attachment, high pulley
steps: Set the pulley slightly above head height and grip the rope with thumbs back.
Step back to create tension; arms extended, palms facing each other.
Pull the rope toward the forehead, separating the hands as you go.
Finish with the elbows high and the hands beside the ears; squeeze, then return slowly.
mistakes: Going too heavy and turning it into a high row.
Letting the elbows drop below the wrists.
Shrugging the upper traps.
tips: The single highest-value corrective for desk posture and shoulder health.
Should be a staple in every ZITLAS program, not an afterthought.
Light weight, high reps, perfect control.
safety: If the traps take over, halve the weight.
progression: Add an external rotation at the end range (a W-pull).
regression: Resistance band pull-apart.

name: Band Pull-Apart
steps: Hold a light band at shoulder height with straight arms, hands shoulder-width.
Keep the ribcage down and the shoulders away from the ears.
Pull the band apart until it touches the sternum.
Squeeze the shoulder blades, then return with control.
mistakes: Bending the elbows.
Arching the lower back.
Shrugging the traps.
tips: The perfect warm-up and desk-break drill — no fatigue cost, high postural payoff.
Can be done 3-5 times per week.
safety: Inspect the band for tears; a snapping band at eye level is dangerous.
progression: Thicker band, or hold the end position for 3 seconds.
regression: Widen the grip to reduce tension.

name: Reverse Fly (Dumbbell)
steps: Hinge forward to 45 degrees or lie chest-down on an incline bench.
Hold light dumbbells with a soft elbow bend, palms facing each other.
Raise the arms out to the sides until level with the torso.
Squeeze the shoulder blades, then lower slowly.
mistakes: Using heavy weight and swinging.
Shrugging so the traps do the work.
Raising the arms above shoulder level.
tips: Rear delts respond to volume and control, not load. Stay light.
Turn the thumbs slightly down to bias the posterior deltoid.
safety: Support the head on the bench to spare the neck.
progression: Add a 2-second hold at the top; then progress to a cable reverse fly.
regression: Band pull-apart.

name: Barbell Shrug
steps: Stand tall holding the bar at arm's length in front of the thighs.
Keep the arms straight and the chin tucked.
Elevate the shoulders straight up toward the ears as high as possible.
Hold for one second at the top, then lower slowly to a full stretch.
mistakes: Rolling the shoulders backwards, which grinds the AC joint for no benefit.
Bending the elbows and pulling with the biceps.
Bouncing the weight with the knees.
tips: Traps elevate the scapula. They do not rotate it. Straight up, straight down.
A 1-second peak hold is worth more than 20 kg of extra load.
Use straps once grip becomes the limiting factor.
safety: Do not roll the shoulders.
progression: Add load with straps, or use a longer 3-second peak hold.
regression: Dumbbell shrug with a lighter load.

name: Rack Pull
secondary: Gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi, forearm flexors
steps: Set the pins so the bar starts at or just below the knees.
Take a deadlift stance and grip; set the lats and brace.
Drive the hips forward and stand tall, keeping the bar against the legs.
Lower back to the pins under control — do not drop the bar.
breathing: Brace at the start, exhale at lockout.
mistakes: Setting the pins so high the movement becomes a shrug.
Hyperextending the spine at the top.
Dropping the bar onto the pins.
tips: Overloads the top half of the deadlift and builds a thick upper back.
Useful for anyone whose deadlift fails above the knee.
safety: Use bar padding on the pins to protect the knurling and reduce noise.
Keep the load appropriate — the shortened range invites ego lifting.
progression: Lower the pins progressively toward the floor.
regression: Romanian deadlift from a shortened range.

name: Good Morning
steps: Rack a light bar high on the traps, feet hip-width, knees softly bent.
Brace hard, then push the hips backwards while the chest travels forward.
Descend until the torso is close to parallel or hamstring tension stops you.
Drive the hips forward and squeeze the glutes to stand.
breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale standing.
mistakes: Loading heavy before the pattern is grooved — the classic injury route.
Rounding the lumbar spine.
Turning it into a squat by bending the knees.
tips: Start with an empty bar. Genuinely. Even strong lifters.
The hips move back, not down.
Superb hamstring and spinal-erector strengthener when respected.
safety: Set safety pins if squatting inside a rack.
This exercise punishes ego more than any other.
progression: Add small load increments (2.5 kg), keeping the spine neutral.
regression: Romanian deadlift, or a dowel-only hip hinge drill.

name: Back Extension (45-Degree)
steps: Set the pad just below the hip crease so the hips can flex freely.
Cross the arms over the chest, spine neutral.
Hinge forward at the hips until a hamstring stretch is felt.
Squeeze the glutes to return to a straight line — do not arch past neutral.
mistakes: Hyperextending at the top, which compresses the lumbar facets.
Rounding the back to gain extra depth.
Adding heavy load before bodyweight is easy for 20 reps.
tips: Stop at a straight line. Extension beyond neutral has no benefit and real cost.
Excellent low-back endurance builder for desk workers and runners.
safety: Do not add a plate until 20 clean bodyweight reps are possible.
progression: Hold a plate against the chest, or slow the eccentric to 4 seconds.
regression: Bird dog or prone hip extension on the floor.

name: Resistance Band Row
equipment: Long resistance band, anchor or feet
steps: Sit on the floor with legs extended and loop the band around the soles.
Hold one end in each hand, arms extended, spine tall.
Row the handles to the lower ribs, driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the shoulder blades, then return under control.
mistakes: Rounding the back and rocking to generate force.
Letting the band snap the arms forward.
tips: The most portable back exercise there is — fits in a hostel drawer or a suitcase.
Shorten the band by wrapping it around the hands to increase resistance.
safety: Ensure the band cannot slip off the feet and recoil into the face.
progression: Thicker band, or a 3-second squeeze at the top.
regression: Standing band row at a lighter tension.

name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
secondary: Lateral deltoid, triceps brachii, upper trapezius, core
steps: Unrack the bar at collarbone height, hands just outside the shoulders.
Brace the abdominals and squeeze the glutes to lock the ribcage down.
Press the bar straight up, moving the head back slightly to clear the chin.
Lock out overhead with the bar over the mid-foot, then lower under control.
breathing: Inhale and brace at the shoulders, exhale past the sticking point.
mistakes: Leaning back and turning it into an incline press.
Pressing around the face instead of moving the head out of the way.
Letting the ribcage flare and the lower back arch.
tips: Glutes and abs are the foundation of a strong overhead press.
Shrug the shoulders up at lockout — that is the correct finish, not a flaw.
safety: Set safety pins at chest height.
Warm the thoracic spine and lats first.
progression: Add 1-2.5 kg per week; then add a push press for overload.
regression: Seated dumbbell shoulder press or landmine press.

name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
steps: Sit with the back supported, dumbbells at shoulder height, palms forward.
Brace the core and keep the ribcage down against the pad.
Press up and slightly inward until the arms are nearly straight.
Lower under control until the elbows drop just below shoulder level.
mistakes: Arching the lower back away from the pad.
Banging the dumbbells together at the top.
Descending so deep the shoulder capsule takes the load.
tips: The safest heavy vertical press for most people — the bench takes the spine out of it.
A neutral (palms-in) grip is gentler on irritated shoulders.
safety: Kick the dumbbells up from the thighs; do not curl them into position.
progression: Add load, or move to a standing barbell press.
regression: Machine shoulder press or seated Arnold press with light weight.

name: Arnold Press
steps: Start seated with dumbbells at chest height, palms facing you (a supinated bottom).
As you press, rotate the palms outward so they face forward at lockout.
Reverse the rotation smoothly on the descent.
mistakes: Rotating too early, before the dumbbells clear the chin.
Using heavy loads that force jerky rotation.
Flaring the ribcage.
tips: The rotation adds range and hits all three deltoid heads in one rep.
Use roughly 70% of your normal dumbbell press load.
safety: Avoid if the rotation causes any pinching at the front of the shoulder.
progression: Add load slowly, or slow the rotation to 3 seconds.
regression: Standard seated dumbbell press.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
steps: Set the seat so the handles sit at shoulder height.
Back flat against the pad, feet planted, core braced.
Press up to near lockout, then return until the handles reach shoulder level.
mistakes: Seat too low, forcing an exaggerated overhead range.
Slamming the stack at the bottom.
tips: Ideal for training to failure alone.
Excellent first vertical press for beginners and seniors.
safety: Adjust the range-of-motion stops if the machine allows.
progression: Progress to dumbbell shoulder press.
regression: Resistance band overhead press, seated.

name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
steps: Stand tall, dumbbells at the sides, soft bend in the elbows.
Lean the torso forward about 10 degrees.
Raise the arms out to the sides until the hands reach shoulder height.
Lower slowly, resisting all the way down.
mistakes: Swinging the weights with hip momentum.
Shrugging the traps so the neck does the lifting.
Raising the hands above shoulder level.
tips: Lead with the elbows, not the hands. Imagine pouring water from a jug.
Light weight, strict form. This is a small muscle with a short lever.
safety: If the traps take over, cut the weight in half.
progression: Add a 2-second hold at the top; then a cable lateral raise for constant tension.
regression: Seated lateral raise (removes momentum) or a band lateral raise.

name: Cable Lateral Raise
steps: Stand side-on to a low pulley; take the handle in the far hand behind the body.
Raise the arm out and up to shoulder height in a wide arc.
Lower slowly against the cable's pull.
mistakes: Leaning away from the stack to cheat.
Shrugging.
Letting the cable snap the arm down.
tips: Cables load the bottom of the raise, where dumbbells give you nothing.
Hold the machine with the free hand for a stable base.
safety: Keep the wrist neutral, not cocked.
progression: Add a slow 4-second eccentric or a drop set.
regression: Dumbbell lateral raise.

name: Front Raise
steps: Stand tall, weight in front of the thighs, palms facing back.
Brace the core so the torso cannot swing.
Raise the arms straight in front to shoulder height.
Lower under control.
mistakes: Swinging the hips and using momentum.
Raising far above shoulder height, which shifts work to the traps.
Doing front raises at all when your program already has plenty of pressing.
tips: Most people do not need direct front-delt work — pressing already covers it.
Include only if the anterior deltoid is a genuine lagging point.
safety: Keep the lower back neutral; brace hard.
progression: Use a plate held with both hands, raised to eye level.
regression: Band front raise with light tension.

name: Upright Row (Wide Grip)
steps: Grip the bar wider than shoulder width — a narrow grip drives impingement.
Stand tall, bar resting against the thighs.
Pull the bar up by driving the elbows out and up, stopping at chest height.
Lower under control.
mistakes: Using a narrow grip and pulling the bar to the chin.
Letting the wrists bend sharply.
Shrugging the bar with the traps.
tips: Stop the elbows at shoulder height. Higher creates internal impingement.
Use a wide grip or switch to a face pull if the shoulders complain.
safety: Discontinue immediately if you feel a pinch at the front of the shoulder.
progression: Add load with a wide grip, or use a cable for smoother resistance.
regression: Face pull or lateral raise — safer and equally effective.

name: Pike Push-Up
secondary: Lateral deltoid, triceps brachii, upper trapezius, serratus anterior
steps: From a push-up position, walk the feet in and pike the hips high.
The torso should be nearly vertical, head between the arms.
Bend the elbows and lower the crown of the head toward the floor.
Press back up to a fully extended arm position.
mistakes: Not piking enough, so it becomes a decline push-up.
Letting the head touch hard.
Flaring the elbows to 90 degrees.
tips: Elevate the feet on a box to make it harder — this is the road to a handstand push-up.
Keep the elbows at roughly 45 degrees from the torso.
safety: Place a folded towel under the head.
Warm the shoulders fully first.
progression: Elevate the feet, then attempt wall-supported handstand push-ups.
regression: Standard push-up or incline pike push-up with hands elevated.

name: Cuban Rotation / External Rotation (Band)
steps: Tuck the elbow against the ribs, bent to 90 degrees, forearm across the belly.
Keeping the elbow pinned, rotate the forearm outward.
Stop when the forearm points straight ahead; do not force further.
Return slowly.
mistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the ribs.
Using far too much resistance.
Rotating the whole torso.
tips: The rotator cuff is an endurance muscle group. Light load, 15-20 reps.
Place a rolled towel between the elbow and ribs to lock the elbow in.
safety: Never load this heavily — the cuff tendons are small.
avoid: Acute rotator cuff tear (post-surgical protocols only under supervision)
progression: Progress to a side-lying dumbbell external rotation.
regression: Isometric external rotation against a wall.

name: Barbell Curl
steps: Stand tall, bar at arm's length, shoulder-width underhand grip.
Pin the elbows to the ribs and brace the core.
Curl the bar up by flexing the elbows only, stopping at chest height.
Lower under control to full extension.
mistakes: Swinging the torso and using the lower back as a lever.
Letting the elbows travel forward, turning it into a front raise.
Cutting the descent short and losing the strongest range.
tips: A curl the torso helps with is not a curl.
Use an EZ bar if straight-bar curls irritate the wrists.
safety: Do not hyperextend the lumbar spine at the top of a heavy set.
progression: Add load, or slow the eccentric to 4 seconds.
regression: Dumbbell curl or cable curl.

name: Dumbbell Curl (Alternating)
steps: Stand tall, dumbbells at the sides, palms facing in.
Curl the right dumbbell, supinating the palm to face up as you rise.
Squeeze at the top, lower slowly, then repeat on the left.
mistakes: Swinging the shoulder forward.
Not supinating fully.
Dropping the weight on the descent.
tips: Full supination maximises biceps shortening at the top.
Alternating gives each arm a rest and lets you use strict form.
safety: Keep the wrists neutral, not bent back.
progression: Curl both arms simultaneously, or add a 2-second peak squeeze.
regression: Seated dumbbell curl with back supported.

name: Hammer Curl
equipment: Two dumbbells or rope on a low pulley
steps: Hold the dumbbells with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
Pin the elbows, curl the weights up without rotating the wrists.
Squeeze, then lower under control.
mistakes: Swinging.
Letting the wrists rotate into a standard curl.
Elbows drifting forward.
tips: The brachialis sits under the biceps — building it pushes the biceps up and adds arm width.
Usually allows 10-15% more load than a supinated curl.
safety: Keep the shoulders down and back.
progression: Add load, or use a rope cable hammer curl for constant tension.
regression: Seated hammer curl with lighter dumbbells.

name: Preacher Curl
equipment: Preacher bench, EZ bar or dumbbell
steps: Set the pad so the armpits rest on the top edge.
Grip the bar underhand, arms resting fully on the pad.
Curl up to roughly 90 degrees of elbow flexion.
Lower slowly until the arms are almost straight — never snap into lockout.
mistakes: Letting the arms slam into full extension at the bottom under load.
Lifting the elbows off the pad.
Going too heavy on a movement built for control.
tips: The preacher bench eliminates all cheating, which is exactly the point.
Stop just short of full lockout to protect the distal biceps tendon.
safety: Have a spotter hand you the bar if going heavy.
Never drop into the bottom with a straight arm.
progression: Progress to single-arm dumbbell preacher curls.
regression: Standing dumbbell curl.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
equipment: Two dumbbells, incline bench at 45-60 degrees
steps: Sit back on a 45-60 degree incline, arms hanging straight down behind the torso.
Curl both dumbbells without letting the elbows move forward.
Squeeze at the top, then lower to a full stretch.
mistakes: Letting the elbows swing forward to reduce the stretch.
Using heavy dumbbells that force a shoulder assist.
tips: The behind-the-body arm position stretches the long head — nothing else does this.
Expect to use less weight than a standing curl. That is correct.
safety: Do not bounce out of the bottom stretch.
progression: Lower the bench angle to increase the stretch.
regression: Standing dumbbell curl.

name: Concentration Curl
steps: Sit on a bench, feet wide; brace the working elbow against the inner thigh.
Let the arm hang straight, dumbbell in hand.
Curl the weight toward the opposite shoulder, supinating fully.
Squeeze for one second, then lower to full extension.
mistakes: Using the leg to push the elbow.
Rocking the torso.
Half-repping at the bottom.
tips: Shows the highest biceps EMG activation of any curl variation.
Great finishing move; keep it light and slow.
safety: Keep the back flat rather than hunched over the knee.
progression: Add a 3-second peak hold.
regression: Seated dumbbell curl with the arm free.

name: Cable Curl
equipment: Cable machine, low pulley, straight or EZ bar
steps: Stand facing a low pulley, grip the bar underhand, elbows pinned.
Curl the bar up to chest height without moving the elbows.
Lower slowly against the cable.
mistakes: Leaning back to complete reps.
Letting the stack pull the arms down fast.
tips: Cables hold tension even at the bottom, where free weights unload.
A rope attachment lets you finish with a hammer-grip squeeze.
safety: Stand far enough back that the stack does not clang.
progression: Add a drop set on the last round.
regression: Resistance band curl.

name: Reverse Curl
steps: Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width, arms straight.
Pin the elbows and curl the bar up, keeping the knuckles pointing up.
Lower slowly to full extension.
mistakes: Letting the wrists collapse into flexion.
Using biceps-curl loads — expect roughly 60% of that weight.
tips: Directly builds the brachioradialis and the wrist extensors.
Excellent for climbers, racquet-sport athletes and anyone with elbow pain.
safety: Keep the wrists rigid and straight.
avoid: Acute lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) — reintroduce gradually
progression: Add load, or use a thick-grip bar.
regression: Dumbbell reverse curl with a lighter load.

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
steps: Lie on a flat bench and grip the bar at roughly shoulder width — not narrower.
Tuck the elbows to about 30 degrees from the torso.
Lower the bar to the lower sternum, keeping the forearms vertical.
Press up, driving through the triceps.
mistakes: Gripping so narrow the wrists are forced into pain.
Flaring the elbows.
Bouncing the bar off the ribs.
tips: Shoulder-width is the sweet spot. Narrower does not add triceps, it adds wrist strain.
The best mass-builder for the triceps because it allows heavy load.
safety: Use a spotter or safety pins.
progression: Add load; then progress to a board press for lockout overload.
regression: Machine triceps press or diamond push-up.

name: Skull Crusher (Lying Triceps Extension)
equipment: EZ bar or dumbbells, flat bench
steps: Lie flat, holding an EZ bar above the chest with a shoulder-width grip.
Angle the arms back slightly so the elbows point toward the ceiling and a little back.
Bend only the elbows, lowering the bar toward the forehead or just behind the head.
Extend the elbows to press the bar back up without moving the upper arms.
mistakes: Letting the upper arms drift back and forth (turning it into a pullover).
Going too heavy and losing control near the head.
Locking out violently and hyperextending the elbows.
tips: Lower behind the head rather than to the forehead to increase long-head stretch.
Use an EZ bar; a straight bar torques the wrists.
safety: Use a spotter.
Never let the bar drop toward the face.
progression: Add load, or move to an overhead cable extension for constant tension.
regression: Dumbbell skull crusher, or a triceps pushdown.

name: Overhead Triceps Extension (Cable or Dumbbell)
equipment: Rope on a low pulley, or one dumbbell
steps: Face away from a low pulley with the rope held overhead behind the head.
Keep the elbows tight and pointing forward, upper arms fixed.
Extend the elbows until the arms are straight overhead.
Lower slowly until a deep stretch is felt behind the arm.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare wide.
Moving the upper arms.
Arching the lower back at lockout.
tips: Only overhead positions fully stretch the triceps long head. Do not skip these.
Brace the abs so the ribcage does not flare.
safety: Keep the load moderate; the overhead position stresses the elbow.
progression: Single-arm version for greater range; or add a 2-second stretch pause.
regression: Seated dumbbell overhead extension with back support.

name: Triceps Pushdown (Rope)
steps: Face a high pulley, rope in both hands, elbows pinned to the ribs.
Push down and separate the rope ends at the bottom.
Squeeze the triceps for one second, then let the rope rise to a full stretch.
mistakes: Letting the elbows drift forward and away from the ribs.
Leaning forward to use bodyweight.
Shrugging the shoulders.
tips: Pinning the elbows is the entire technique. Everything else is detail.
Spreading the rope at the bottom adds a peak contraction.
safety: Do not let the stack pull the arms up quickly.
progression: Drop set, or switch to a single-arm reverse-grip pushdown.
regression: Resistance band pushdown.

name: Triceps Dip (Bench)
steps: Sit on the edge of a bench, hands beside the hips, fingers pointing forward.
Slide the hips off the edge, legs extended or knees bent.
Lower the body by bending the elbows straight back to roughly 90 degrees.
Press back up without locking out aggressively.
mistakes: Descending too deep, which forces the shoulder into extreme extension.
Letting the hips drift away from the bench.
Flaring the elbows outward.
tips: Stop at 90 degrees of elbow bend. Deeper is a shoulder injury waiting to happen.
Bend the knees to regress; extend the legs or add a plate to progress.
safety: Do not use a rolling chair.
Stop at once if the front of the shoulder pinches.
progression: Elevate the feet, or rest a plate on the thighs.
regression: Bend the knees and keep the feet close to the bench.

name: Parallel Bar Triceps Dip
steps: Mount the bars with the arms locked and the torso upright.
Keep the elbows tucked close to the ribs throughout.
Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press back up, staying vertical (a forward lean shifts load to the chest).
mistakes: Leaning forward, which converts it into a chest dip.
Descending past parallel.
Shrugging at the bottom.
tips: Torso upright, elbows in. That is the triceps version.
Depress the shoulder blades hard at the top of every rep.
safety: Progress with assisted dips before attempting bodyweight.
progression: Add a dip belt with 5-10 kg.
regression: Band-assisted dip or bench dip.

name: Diamond Push-Up (Triceps Focus)
steps: Place the hands under the sternum, index fingers and thumbs touching.
Hold a rigid plank; squeeze the glutes.
Lower with the elbows tracking backwards along the ribs.
Press up to lockout.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows.
Placing the hands too far forward.
Hips rising before the chest.
tips: Keep the elbows brushing the ribcage — that is what makes it a triceps move.
If the wrists hurt, do it on fists or push-up handles.
safety: Warm the wrists thoroughly.
progression: Elevate the feet or wear a weight vest.
regression: Diamond push-up with the knees on the floor.

name: Resistance Band Triceps Pushdown
equipment: Resistance band, high anchor (door or bar)
steps: Anchor a band overhead and grip both ends with the elbows pinned.
Push down until the arms are straight, squeezing at the bottom.
Let the band draw the hands back up slowly.
mistakes: Elbows drifting forward.
Standing too close so the band has no tension.
tips: Step further from the anchor to increase resistance.
The perfect hostel or hotel-room triceps builder.
safety: Inspect the band before each session.
progression: Thicker band or a single-arm version.
regression: Diamond push-up with knees down.

name: Wrist Curl (Flexion)
steps: Sit and rest the forearms on the thighs, palms facing up, wrists past the knees.
Let the bar roll down to the fingertips.
Curl the fingers closed, then flex the wrist upward as far as possible.
Lower slowly to a full stretch.
mistakes: Using heavy weight and bouncing the wrist.
Lifting the forearms off the thighs.
Skipping the finger roll.
tips: The finger roll at the bottom doubles the range and the grip benefit.
High reps (15-20) suit the forearms' fibre composition.
safety: Stop at once if you feel numbness or tingling into the hand.
progression: Add load slowly, or use a wrist roller.
regression: Squeeze a stress ball or hand gripper.

name: Wrist Extension
steps: Rest the forearm on the thigh, palm facing down, wrist past the knee.
Lower the hand as far as comfortable.
Lift the back of the hand toward the ceiling, then lower slowly.
mistakes: Loading far too heavily.
Lifting the forearm off the support.
tips: The single most useful drill for tennis elbow prevention and rehab.
Use 1-2 kg. That is genuinely enough.
safety: Progress very slowly if you have current elbow pain.
progression: Add a 3-second eccentric — the eccentric drives tendon adaptation.
regression: Rubber-band finger extension.

name: Farmer's Carry
equipment: Two heavy dumbbells, kettlebells or farmer's handles
steps: Deadlift a heavy weight into each hand and stand tall.
Set the shoulders back and down, ribcage stacked over the pelvis.
Walk with controlled, normal-length steps.
Set the weights down under control — do not drop them.
breathing: Breathe shallowly and continuously; never hold your breath for the whole carry.
mistakes: Leaning to one side.
Shrugging the shoulders up to the ears.
Taking tiny shuffling steps.
tips: The most transferable exercise in the entire database — grip, core, posture, work capacity.
Distance or time, not reps. 30-40 m per set is a good target.
safety: Clear the walking path.
Use straps only once grip is the true limiter.
progression: Add load, or switch to a single-arm suitcase carry for anti-lateral-flexion.
regression: Lighter dumbbells, shorter distance.

name: Suitcase Carry
steps: Hold a single heavy weight in one hand at the side.
Stand perfectly tall — resist the pull to lean toward the weight.
Walk 20-30 m maintaining level shoulders and hips.
Switch hands and repeat.
mistakes: Leaning toward or away from the weight.
Letting the shoulder on the loaded side drop.
Rotating the pelvis.
tips: This is a core exercise disguised as a grip exercise.
Film yourself from the front once — most people lean far more than they think.
safety: Start with about 25% of bodyweight in one hand.
progression: Add load, or perform an overhead waiter's carry.
regression: Reduce the weight and shorten the distance.

name: Barbell Back Squat
secondary: Adductor magnus, erector spinae, hamstrings, core
steps: Set the bar on the upper traps (high bar) or across the rear delts (low bar).
Unrack, take two steps back, feet shoulder-width, toes turned out 15-30 degrees.
Brace the abdominals, break at the hips and knees together, and descend.
Reach at least parallel — hip crease level with the knee — then drive the floor away.
Stand tall without hyperextending the lower back.
breathing: Big breath in and brace at the top; hold through the descent, exhale on the way up.
mistakes: Knees caving inward under load (valgus collapse).
The hips shooting up first, turning the squat into a good morning.
Heels lifting off the floor.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom (butt wink under load).
tips: Screw the feet into the floor to create external rotation torque at the hips.
The bar must stay over the mid-foot for the entire rep.
Depth is limited by ankle and hip mobility, not by willpower.
safety: Always set the safety pins just below your bottom position.
Never squat with a rounded lower back under load.
avoid: Acute knee or lower back injury
Severe ankle mobility restriction (fix the mobility first)
progression: Add 2.5 kg per session; then add pause squats and tempo squats.
regression: Goblet squat or box squat to a controlled depth.

name: Front Squat
secondary: Gluteus maximus, erector spinae, upper back, core
steps: Rack the bar across the front delts, fingers under the bar, elbows high.
Keep the elbows pointing forward throughout — dropping them dumps the bar.
Descend with a vertical torso, knees travelling forward over the toes.
Drive up out of the hole, keeping the chest tall.
breathing: Brace at the top, exhale on the ascent.
mistakes: Elbows dropping, which rounds the upper back and drops the bar.
Attempting a full grip when wrist mobility does not allow it.
Leaning forward like a back squat.
tips: Use a two- or three-finger grip if wrist mobility is limited; the shelf is the delts, not the hands.
Front squats punish forward lean instantly — an excellent form teacher.
safety: Learn to dump the bar forward safely before going heavy.
Set the safeties.
progression: Add load; then progress to pause front squats.
regression: Goblet squat or Zercher squat.

name: Goblet Squat
steps: Hold a kettlebell by the horns at chest height, elbows tucked in.
Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
Squat down between the legs, keeping the chest tall and the elbows inside the knees.
Pause at the bottom, then drive up through the whole foot.
mistakes: Letting the weight pull the chest forward.
Knees caving in.
Bouncing out of the bottom.
tips: The counterweight at the chest automatically teaches an upright torso.
The single best squat teaching tool. Every beginner should start here.
Use the elbows to gently push the knees out at the bottom.
safety: Choose a weight you can control for 10 clean reps.
progression: Add load, then move to a front or back squat.
regression: Bodyweight box squat to a chair.

name: Bodyweight Squat
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out, arms extended forward for balance.
Push the hips back and down, keeping the chest up.
Descend until the thighs are parallel to the floor, or as low as control allows.
Drive through the whole foot to stand tall.
mistakes: Knees caving inward.
Heels lifting.
Rounding the lower back to reach depth.
tips: Push the knees out over the second and third toes.
If the heels lift, place a 2 cm plate or book under them while you fix ankle mobility.
safety: Squat to a chair if balance is uncertain.
avoid: Severe balance impairment (use a chair squat instead)
progression: Add tempo, then a goblet squat, then jump squats.
regression: Box squat to a chair, standing back up with hands on the thighs.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
steps: Place the top of the rear foot on a bench roughly knee height.
Step the front foot far enough forward that the shin stays near vertical at the bottom.
Lower straight down until the rear knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive up through the front heel; the rear leg only balances.
mistakes: Front foot too close, forcing the knee far past the toes.
Pushing off the rear foot.
Torso collapsing forward under load.
tips: Shift the torso forward slightly to bias the glutes; stay upright to bias the quads.
Brutally effective, and it exposes side-to-side imbalances that squats hide.
Start with bodyweight only — most people cannot do 10 clean reps.
safety: Use a low box first.
Hold a rack for balance if needed.
progression: Add dumbbells, then a front-racked barbell.
regression: Static split squat with both feet on the floor.

name: Reverse Lunge
steps: Stand tall, feet hip-width.
Step one foot back and lower until both knees reach about 90 degrees.
Keep the front shin vertical and the torso upright.
Drive through the front heel to return to standing.
mistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Stepping back too short, crowding the front knee.
Slamming the rear knee into the floor.
tips: Reverse lunges load the knee less than forward lunges — the default choice for knee pain.
Keep 80% of the weight in the front leg.
safety: Perform near a wall if balance is a concern.
progression: Add dumbbells; then progress to walking lunges or deficit reverse lunges.
regression: Step-up to a low box, or a static split squat.

name: Walking Lunge
steps: Step forward into a lunge, lowering until both knees are at 90 degrees.
Drive through the front heel and bring the rear foot forward into the next lunge.
Keep the torso tall and the steps consistent in length.
breathing: Exhale as you rise out of each lunge.
mistakes: Short steps, which push the knee far past the toes.
Torso pitching forward.
Losing balance and staggering sideways.
tips: A long stride biases the glutes; a shorter stride biases the quads.
Excellent metabolic conditioning when done for distance.
safety: Clear a straight path.
Do not perform on slippery flooring.
progression: Add dumbbells or a front-racked barbell.
regression: Reverse lunge in place.

name: Step-Up
equipment: Box, bench or step; dumbbells optional
steps: Place one full foot on a box roughly knee height.
Drive through that heel to stand fully on top of the box.
Control the descent, tapping the floor lightly with the other foot.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
breathing: Exhale stepping up, inhale stepping down.
mistakes: Pushing off the bottom leg to help.
Using a box so high the hip has to hike.
Dropping down with no eccentric control.
tips: The bottom foot should be able to hover — that proves the top leg is doing the work.
Lower the box for knee pain; raise it for a glute emphasis.
Superb for seniors, runners and rehab.
safety: Test the box for stability.
Keep the full foot on the box, not just the toes.
progression: Raise the box or add dumbbells.
regression: Lower the box to 15-20 cm.

name: Leg Press
steps: Sit with the back and hips flat against the pad, feet shoulder-width on the platform.
Release the safeties and lower the platform until the knees reach about 90 degrees.
Stop before the lower back lifts off the pad.
Press back up without locking the knees hard.
mistakes: Descending so deep the pelvis tucks and the lumbar spine rounds.
Snapping the knees into full lockout.
Placing the hands on the knees during the press.
tips: Range of motion is capped by where the lower back lifts, not by the machine's travel.
High foot placement biases glutes and hamstrings; low placement biases quads.
The safest way to load the legs heavily without spinal compression.
safety: Engage the safety catches before dismounting.
Never let the platform crash down.
progression: Add load, or switch to a single-leg press.
regression: Goblet squat with light load.

name: Hack Squat (Machine)
steps: Set the shoulders under the pads, back flat against the backrest.
Place the feet mid-platform, shoulder-width.
Descend until the thighs pass parallel, knees tracking over the toes.
Drive up through the whole foot without locking out hard.
mistakes: Placing the feet too low, which shears the knee.
Letting the heels lift.
Bouncing at the bottom.
tips: The fixed path lets you push closer to failure than a free squat.
Feet slightly forward protects the knees; feet low maximises quad stretch.
safety: Engage the safety handles before dismounting.
progression: Add load, or add a 3-second pause at the bottom.
regression: Leg press.

name: Leg Extension
steps: Adjust the seat so the knee joint lines up with the machine's pivot.
Set the ankle pad just above the shoe line.
Extend the knees until the legs are straight; squeeze for one second.
Lower slowly under control.
mistakes: Slamming the stack down.
Using momentum from the hips.
Loading so heavily that the knee is jerked into extension.
tips: The only exercise that isolates the quadriceps completely.
Valuable for VMO strength and knee rehab under professional guidance.
Moderate load, controlled tempo, 12-15 reps.
safety: Align the joint pivot correctly — misalignment is what gives this exercise its bad reputation.
progression: Add a 2-second squeeze at lockout, or a slow 4-second eccentric.
regression: Reduce load and range; or perform a seated knee extension against a band.

name: Sissy Squat
equipment: None, or a sissy squat bench
steps: Hold a support with one hand; rise onto the balls of the feet.
Drive the knees forward while leaning the torso backwards.
Keep the hips, knees and shoulders in one straight line.
Descend as far as knee comfort allows, then squeeze back up.
mistakes: Bending at the hips instead of staying in a straight line.
Going too deep too soon.
Attempting it with existing knee pain.
tips: A knees-over-toes movement that, trained progressively, builds knee resilience.
Start with a very small range — 20 degrees of knee bend — and add slowly.
safety: Progress over months, not weeks.
Never train through sharp knee pain.
progression: Reduce hand support, then add a weight plate on the chest.
regression: Kneeling quad stretch with a slight backward lean.

name: Wall Sit
steps: Stand with the back flat against a wall, feet about 50 cm forward.
Slide down until the knees and hips are both at 90 degrees.
Keep the whole back in contact with the wall and the weight in the heels.
Hold for the prescribed time.
breathing: Breathe normally and continuously — never hold your breath.
mistakes: Holding the breath, which spikes blood pressure.
Letting the knees drift past the toes.
Resting the hands on the thighs.
tips: An isometric hold with almost zero joint load — ideal for knee rehab.
Start at 20 seconds and build to 60.
safety: Do not perform to failure if you have hypertension.
progression: Extend the hold, or add a weight plate to the lap.
regression: Reduce the depth so the knee angle is 120 degrees.

name: Romanian Deadlift (Single Leg)
secondary: Erector spinae, gluteus medius, ankle stabilisers
