steps: Stand on one leg, holding a weight in the opposite hand.
Hinge at the hip, letting the free leg extend straight behind as a counterbalance.
Keep the hips square — do not let the free hip rotate open.
Return to standing by squeezing the glute of the standing leg.
mistakes: Rotating the pelvis open.
Rounding the lower back.
Bending the standing knee excessively.
tips: Place a hand on a wall until balance improves.
The best exercise for hamstring asymmetry and hamstring-strain prevention in runners.
safety: Start with bodyweight only.
progression: Increase load, then remove the hand support entirely.
regression: Two-leg Romanian deadlift.

name: Lying Leg Curl
steps: Lie face down with the knee joint aligned with the machine pivot.
Set the ankle pad just above the heels.
Curl the heels toward the glutes, squeezing at the top.
Lower slowly to near full knee extension.
mistakes: Lifting the hips off the pad to gain leverage.
Slamming the stack down.
Cutting the range short at the bottom.
tips: Point the toes to bias the hamstrings; flex them to involve the calves.
Essential counterbalance to squat-heavy programming.
safety: Keep the hips pinned to the pad.
progression: Add load, or perform single-leg curls.
regression: Nordic curl eccentric-only, or a stability ball leg curl.

name: Seated Leg Curl
steps: Set the back pad and align the knees with the machine pivot.
Secure the thigh pad firmly across the quads.
Curl the heels down and back, then return slowly.
mistakes: Loose thigh pad letting the hips lift.
Explosive, bouncy reps.
tips: The seated position holds the hip flexed, which lengthens the hamstring — research shows this trains the muscle in the stretched position more effectively than lying curls.
Pair with a lying curl for full coverage.
safety: Do not let the pad crash at the end of the set.
progression: Add load or a 3-second eccentric.
regression: Lying leg curl.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
equipment: Partner, Nordic bench, or loaded barbell to pin the ankles
steps: Kneel on a pad with the ankles secured firmly behind you.
Keep the body in a straight line from knee to shoulder — no hip hinge.
Lower the torso toward the floor as slowly as possible, resisting with the hamstrings.
Catch yourself with the hands and push back to the start.
breathing: Inhale on the descent, exhale on the push back.
mistakes: Hinging at the hips to shorten the lever.
Dropping quickly instead of resisting.
Doing high volume — this causes severe soreness.
tips: Reduces hamstring injury rates by roughly half in athlete populations — the strongest evidence base of any single exercise.
Start with 2 sets of 3 reps. Soreness after the first session is severe.
Use a band around the chest for assistance in early weeks.
safety: Place a pad under the knees.
Always have hands ready to catch the floor.
progression: Increase range before adding reps; eventually add a slow concentric.
regression: Band-assisted Nordic, or a razor curl with hip support.

name: Glute-Ham Raise
steps: Set the foot plate so the knees sit just behind the pad.
Start with the torso upright, body straight from knee to head.
Lower slowly under hamstring control until the torso is horizontal.
Curl back up using the hamstrings, keeping the hips extended.
mistakes: Hinging at the hips.
Using a hip-extension swing to return.
Attempting full reps before the eccentric is mastered.
tips: Bridges the gap between a back extension and a Nordic curl.
Place the hands on the chest to increase difficulty.
safety: Set the machine correctly — knee position determines the leverage.
avoid: Acute hamstring or lower back injury
progression: Hold a plate at the chest.
regression: Perform eccentric-only, or a back extension.

name: Barbell Hip Thrust
steps: Sit on the floor with the upper back against a bench, bar across the hips on a pad.
Feet flat, shins vertical at the top of the movement, chin tucked.
Drive through the heels and extend the hips until the torso is parallel to the floor.
Squeeze the glutes hard for one second, then lower under control.
mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back instead of extending the hips.
Placing the feet too close or too far, which recruits quads or hamstrings.
Letting the chin lift and the neck extend.
tips: Ribs down, chin tucked, posterior pelvic tilt at the top. That is the whole exercise.
Produces the highest gluteus maximus activation of any loaded movement.
A 1-second pause at lockout is non-negotiable.
safety: Use a thick bar pad.
Roll the bar into position; do not drop it onto the hips.
progression: Add load; then progress to a single-leg hip thrust.
regression: Glute bridge from the floor.

name: Glute Bridge
equipment: None, or a dumbbell across the hips
steps: Lie on the back, knees bent, feet flat and hip-width, heels close to the glutes.
Tuck the pelvis slightly and brace the abdominals.
Drive through the heels to lift the hips until knees, hips and shoulders align.
Squeeze for two seconds, then lower slowly.
mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top instead of squeezing the glutes.
Pushing through the toes.
Letting the knees fall inward.
tips: If you feel it in the hamstrings, move the heels closer to the glutes.
The safest glute exercise available — suitable for post-partum, seniors and back pain.
Add a band around the knees to include the gluteus medius.
safety: Keep the ribs down; do not hyperextend the spine.
progression: Add a dumbbell, then a single-leg version, then a barbell hip thrust.
regression: Reduce range; lift only halfway.

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
steps: Set up as for a hip thrust but with one foot planted and the other leg lifted.
Keep the lifted knee pulled toward the chest to stop the hip flexor cheating.
Drive up through the planted heel and squeeze at the top.
Keep the pelvis perfectly level — do not let one hip drop.
mistakes: Letting the pelvis rotate or drop on one side.
Hyperextending the lower back.
Pushing through the toes.
tips: Exposes glute asymmetry that bilateral thrusts hide.
Excellent for runners and single-leg sport athletes.
safety: Master the bilateral hip thrust first.
progression: Add a dumbbell across the hip.
regression: Two-leg glute bridge.

name: Cable Kickback
equipment: Cable machine, ankle strap, low pulley
steps: Attach the strap to one ankle and face the low pulley, holding the frame.
Hinge forward slightly, brace the core, and keep the working leg slightly bent.
Drive the leg straight back, squeezing the glute; stop when the hip is extended.
Return slowly without letting the stack touch down.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to gain extra range.
Swinging the leg with momentum.
Rotating the pelvis.
tips: Hip extension ends at neutral. Anything beyond comes from the spine.
Great glute isolation, but never a substitute for hip thrusts or squats.
safety: Brace hard; the lumbar spine takes over easily here.
progression: Add a 2-second squeeze.
regression: Standing band kickback with lighter tension.

name: Banded Lateral Walk
steps: Place a mini band just above the knees or around the ankles.
Adopt a quarter-squat with feet hip-width and toes forward.
Step sideways, leading with the heel, keeping tension in the band.
Take controlled steps without letting the trailing foot snap in.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave in.
Standing too upright.
Bouncing the trailing leg in.
tips: The premier gluteus medius drill — critical for knee valgus and runner's knee.
Band at the ankles is harder than band above the knees.
Keep the toes pointing forward, not turned out.
safety: Stop if you feel it in the outside of the thigh (TFL) rather than the side of the hip.
progression: Move the band to the ankles, or use a heavier band.
regression: Side-lying clamshell.

name: Clamshell
secondary: Gluteus minimus, deep hip external rotators
steps: Lie on one side, knees bent to 45 degrees, feet stacked, hips stacked.
Place a band above the knees if available.
Keeping the feet together, rotate the top knee upward.
Stop before the pelvis rolls backwards; lower slowly.
mistakes: Rolling the pelvis back to gain more range.
Rushing the reps.
Using too heavy a band.
tips: Place a hand on the top hip; if it rolls, you have gone too far.
The go-to entry point for hip stability in rehab and post-partum programming.
safety: Keep the movement small and precise.
avoid: Acute hip bursitis (may need reduced range)
progression: Add a band, then progress to a side-lying hip abduction.
regression: Perform without a band.

name: Standing Calf Raise
equipment: Calf raise machine, Smith machine, or a step
steps: Stand with the balls of the feet on a step, heels hanging free.
Keep the knees straight (but not locked) throughout.
Rise onto the toes as high as possible; squeeze for one second.
Lower slowly until a deep stretch is felt at the bottom.
mistakes: Bouncing out of the bottom stretch using the Achilles tendon's elasticity.
Cutting the range short at the top.
Bending the knees (which turns it into a soleus exercise).
tips: A straight knee targets the gastrocnemius; a bent knee targets the soleus. Train both.
1-second pause at the top and bottom. The calves respond to time under tension.
safety: Hold a support for balance.
Do not bounce with a history of Achilles issues.
progression: Add load, or progress to single-leg calf raises.
regression: Flat-ground calf raise without the deficit.

name: Seated Calf Raise
equipment: Seated calf raise machine, or a dumbbell on the knees
steps: Sit with the balls of the feet on the platform and the pad across the lower thighs.
Knees bent to 90 degrees throughout.
Press through the toes to raise the heels; squeeze at the top.
Lower slowly to a full stretch.
mistakes: Bouncing.
Short range at the bottom.
Skipping the exercise entirely, which most lifters do.
tips: The soleus is the single largest contributor to standing calf endurance and Achilles resilience.
Higher reps (15-25) work best here.
Runners and cricketers should not neglect this.
safety: Ensure the pad is secure before releasing the safety.
progression: Add load, or hold the top for 3 seconds.
regression: Seated bodyweight heel raise.

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
steps: Stand on one foot with the ball of the foot on a step, holding a wall.
Lower the heel until a strong calf stretch is felt.
Rise as high as possible onto the toe; hold one second.
Complete all reps, then switch.
mistakes: Using the wall to pull yourself up.
Rushing.
Rolling to the outside of the foot.
tips: Being able to perform 25 single-leg raises is a common return-to-run benchmark.
Drive through the big toe, not the little toe.
safety: Progress gradually if you have Achilles history.
progression: Hold a dumbbell in the free hand.
regression: Two-leg calf raise.

name: Tibialis Raise
steps: Lean the upper back against a wall with the heels 30-40 cm from it.
Keep the legs straight and the heels planted.
Lift the toes and forefoot toward the shins as high as possible.
Lower slowly.
mistakes: Bending the knees.
Rushing through the range.
Placing the feet too close to the wall.
tips: Directly reduces shin splint risk and improves ankle dorsiflexion under load.
Highly recommended for runners, footballers and cricketers.
safety: Expect a strong burn — that is normal.
avoid: Acute anterior compartment syndrome (medical emergency; seek care)
progression: Move the heels further from the wall, or add a tib bar.
regression: Seated toe raises with no wall lean.

name: Plank
steps: Rest on the forearms and toes, elbows directly under the shoulders.
Form a straight line from head to heels — no sagging, no piking.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the abdominals as if bracing for a punch.
Breathe steadily and hold the position for the prescribed time.
breathing: Breathe normally throughout; never hold the breath.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag, which loads the lumbar spine.
Piking the hips up to make it easier.
Holding the breath instead of breathing through the hold.
tips: A plank is a moving target, not a static one — actively pull the elbows toward the toes to keep tension high.
30 quality seconds beats 2 poor minutes.
safety: Stop the set the instant the hips sag — do not chase the clock.
progression: Add a shoulder tap, a weighted plate, or progress to a long-lever plank.
regression: Perform on the knees, or elevate the hands on a bench.

name: Side Plank
steps: Lie on one side, propped on the forearm with the elbow under the shoulder.
Stack the feet, or stagger them for more stability.
Lift the hips until the body forms a straight line.
Hold, keeping the hips high and square — do not let them sag or rotate.
mistakes: Letting the hips drop toward the floor.
Rotating the top shoulder forward.
Holding the head in a strained position.
tips: This trains anti-lateral-flexion — resisting side-bending — which the plank does not address.
Stagger the feet front-to-back for an easier, more stable variant.
safety: Support the head with the free arm if the neck complains.
progression: Lift the top leg, or add a rotation reaching under the torso.
regression: Perform with the top knee bent and resting on the floor.

name: Dead Bug
steps: Lie on the back, arms reaching to the ceiling, knees bent 90 degrees over the hips.
Press the lower back flat into the floor and keep it there for the whole set.
Slowly extend one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor.
Return to the start and repeat on the other side without the back arching.
breathing: Exhale extending the limbs, inhale returning.
mistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor as the limbs extend.
Moving too fast for the core to control.
Letting the extending leg or arm touch down and rest.
tips: The lower back staying flat is the entire point — treat every rep as a test, not a rep count.
Widely used in physiotherapy as the safest entry point for core control.
safety: Stop extending the limb the moment the back starts to arch.
progression: Extend the limbs further, or add ankle weights.
regression: Move only the arms, or only the legs, not both together.

name: Bird Dog
steps: Start on hands and knees, spine neutral, hands under shoulders, knees under hips.
Brace the core, then extend the right arm and left leg simultaneously.
Keep the hips and shoulders square to the floor — no rotation.
Return with control and repeat on the opposite side.
mistakes: Rotating the hips as the leg extends.
Arching the lower back to gain height.
Moving too quickly to control the torso.
tips: Balance a light object on the lower back to give instant feedback on stability.
A cornerstone rehab movement for lower back pain populations.
safety: Keep movements slow and controlled.
progression: Add a 2-second hold at extension, or add light ankle/wrist weights.
regression: Extend only the arm or only the leg, not both.

name: Hanging Leg Raise
steps: Hang from a bar with a full grip, shoulders engaged (not a dead hang).
Brace the core and posteriorly tilt the pelvis before the legs move.
Raise the legs, straight if possible, until at least parallel to the floor.
Lower with control — do not let momentum swing the body.
mistakes: Swinging the body to throw the legs up.
Using hip flexors only, without the posterior pelvic tilt.
Losing grip and dropping.
tips: The tilt of the pelvis, not the height of the legs, is what makes this a true ab exercise.
Bend the knees to regress instantly if the straight-leg version breaks form.
safety: Build grip and shoulder strength on dead hangs first.
progression: Add ankle weights, or progress to toes-to-bar.
regression: Bent-knee (bicycle) hanging raise, or a captain's chair raise.

name: Captain's Chair Leg Raise
equipment: Captain's chair / vertical knee raise station
steps: Support the body on the forearm pads, back flat against the backrest.
Brace the core and posteriorly tilt the pelvis.
Raise the knees toward the chest, curling the pelvis under.
Lower with control, stopping just short of the legs swinging.
mistakes: Swinging the legs using momentum.
Arching the lower back away from the pad.
Using tiny, incomplete range.
tips: A superb, back-supported entry point before hanging raises.
Focus on the pelvis curling under, not just the knees lifting.
safety: Keep the back flat against the pad throughout.
progression: Straighten the legs, or add ankle weights.
regression: Reduce the range, lifting only to hip height.

name: Reverse Crunch
steps: Lie on the back, knees bent 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor.
Press the lower back into the floor and keep it there.
Curl the knees toward the chest by tilting the pelvis, not by swinging the legs.
Lower under control without letting the back arch or the feet touch down hard.
mistakes: Using leg-swing momentum instead of a pelvis curl.
Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Yanking the head and neck to assist.
tips: Picture drawing the hips toward the ribs, not the knees toward the chest.
A safe, effective lower-ab builder for beginners.
safety: Keep the movement slow and controlled — momentum defeats the purpose.
progression: Add ankle weights, or progress to a hanging or captain's chair raise.
regression: Perform with bent knees kept close to the chest throughout (smaller range).

name: Bicycle Crunch
steps: Lie on the back, hands lightly behind the head, knees bent and lifted.
Curl the torso up slightly, bringing the right elbow toward the left knee.
Extend the right leg straight as the left knee draws in.
Alternate sides in a slow, controlled pedalling motion.
breathing: Exhale on each crunch, inhale between sides.
mistakes: Yanking the neck with the hands.
Moving so fast the range becomes tiny and momentum-driven.
Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
tips: Slow this down deliberately — most people rush it and get little from it.
The elbow should reach toward the knee, not touch it; a small twist is enough.
safety: Keep the hands as a light cradle, not a pulling force on the neck.
progression: Slow the tempo to a 3-second rotation per side.
regression: Perform without lifting the shoulders, just alternating knee drives.

name: Russian Twist
equipment: Bodyweight, or a light plate/medicine ball
steps: Sit with the knees bent, torso leaned back to about 45 degrees, feet lifted or grounded.
Hold the hands together (or a light weight) at the chest.
Rotate the torso to touch the floor beside one hip, then the other.
Keep the chest tall throughout the rotation — do not round forward.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further.
Moving so fast the rotation becomes a blur with no control.
Using far too heavy a weight for a rotational movement.
tips: Feet on the floor is a legitimate and often better regression — it is not cheating.
This is a rotation exercise, not a distance-touched exercise.
safety: Keep the weight light; heavy loaded spinal rotation carries real disc-injury risk.
progression: Lift the feet off the floor, or add light load.
regression: Keep the feet planted and reduce the rotation range.

name: Pallof Press
equipment: Cable machine or resistance band, anchored at chest height
steps: Stand side-on to the anchor, cable/band held at the sternum with both hands.
Step out until there is real tension in the line.
Press the hands straight out in front of the chest, resisting the pull to rotate.
Hold for a beat, then return with control.
mistakes: Letting the torso rotate toward the anchor.
Pressing with bent elbows instead of full extension.
Standing too close, removing the challenge.
tips: This is anti-rotation, not rotation — the goal is to stay perfectly still while the cable tries to twist you.
One of the best core exercises for rotational-sport athletes, including cricket.
safety: Keep the stance athletic and grounded.
progression: Step further out, add a reverse lunge, or increase the load.
regression: Reduce the distance from the anchor.

name: Hollow Body Hold
steps: Lie on the back, press the lower back firmly into the floor.
Raise the shoulders and legs a few inches off the ground simultaneously.
Reach the arms overhead, forming a gentle banana shape.
Hold, keeping the lower back glued to the floor the entire time.
breathing: Breathe shallowly and continuously; do not hold the breath.
mistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor — this is the most common failure.
Raising the legs too high, which reduces the challenge.
Straining the neck by looking up.
tips: A gymnastics staple — if the back lifts off the floor, the hold has technically ended.
Bend the knees to instantly regress if the lower back cannot stay down.
safety: Stop the moment the lower back arches; do not push through.
progression: Extend the hold, or add a rock (hollow body rocks).
regression: Bend the knees and keep the arms at the sides.

name: Cable Crunch
equipment: Cable machine, rope attachment, high pulley
steps: Kneel below a high pulley, rope held beside the head, elbows fixed near the ears.
Hinge from the hips first, then curl the spine, bringing the elbows toward the thighs.
Focus on flexing the spine — a true crunch, not a hip hinge.
Return under control to a full stretch.
mistakes: Hinging at the hips instead of flexing the spine — turns it into a bad-form good morning.
Using the arms to pull instead of the abs to curl.
Choosing far too much weight.
tips: The single best loaded ab exercise — resistance increases as the muscle shortens, matching its strength curve.
Keep the hips relatively still; the movement comes from the spine.
safety: Avoid loading through a rounded, unwarmed spine.
progression: Add load progressively.
regression: Bodyweight crunch on the floor.

name: Standard Crunch
steps: Lie on the back, knees bent, feet flat, hands lightly supporting the head.
Press the lower back into the floor.
Curl the shoulder blades a few inches off the floor by flexing the spine.
Lower slowly without fully relaxing between reps.
mistakes: Pulling on the neck with the hands.
Using hip flexors to yank the torso up.
Coming up too far, past where the abs are doing the work.
tips: Full sit-ups are not necessary for ab development — a few inches of true spinal flexion is enough.
Exhale fully at the top to intensify the contraction.
safety: Keep the chin off the chest — a fist's gap under the jaw.
avoid: Acute neck or lower back pain
progression: Add a weight plate on the chest, or move to a cable crunch.
regression: Perform with the arms crossed over the chest instead of behind the head.

name: Ab Wheel Rollout
steps: Kneel on a pad, hands gripping the wheel directly under the shoulders.
Brace the core hard before initiating any movement.
Roll forward slowly, keeping the spine in a single neutral line — no sagging.
Stop before the lower back is at risk of arching, then pull back to the start.
breathing: Inhale rolling out, exhale pulling back.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor at full extension.
Rolling out further than current core strength supports.
Using the arms to pull back instead of the abs.
tips: The range should be earned, not forced — most people should start with partial rollouts.
This loads the abdominals in a long, anti-extension position that few other exercises reach.
safety: Master planks and ab rollouts against a wall before free rollouts.
Stop immediately if the lower back arches.
progression: Increase the rollout distance progressively toward full extension.
regression: Rollout from the knees with a small range, or use a barbell instead of a wheel for more stability.

name: Mountain Climber
steps: Start in a push-up plank position, hands under the shoulders.
Brace the core to keep the hips level and still.
Drive one knee toward the chest, then quickly switch legs.
Continue at a controlled but brisk pace, keeping the hips down throughout.
breathing: Breathe rhythmically with the leg drive.
mistakes: Letting the hips pike up, which turns it into a poor plank.
Bouncing the hips up and down instead of staying level.
Losing the plank as fatigue sets in — quality drops fast here.
tips: Slow the tempo down if the hips cannot stay stable — speed is not the goal, control is.
A genuinely excellent core-and-cardio hybrid for HIIT circuits.
safety: Keep the wrists warm; place hands on an elevated surface if wrist pain occurs.
progression: Increase speed, or elevate the hands on a lower surface.
regression: Slow deliberate reps, or elevate the hands on a bench.

name: Woodchopper (Cable, High to Low)
equipment: Cable machine, high pulley, rope or handle
steps: Stand side-on to a high pulley, feet shoulder-width, holding the handle with both hands.
Rotate the torso and pull the handle diagonally down and across the body.
Pivot the back foot naturally as the hips rotate.
Return along the same diagonal path under control.
mistakes: Using only the arms without hip and torso rotation.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom.
Choosing a weight too heavy to control the rotation.
tips: This trains rotational power in a pattern that mirrors throwing, swinging a bat, or bowling.
Drive the rotation from the hips, not the shoulders.
safety: Warm up the spine with cat-cow before loading rotation.
progression: Add load, or perform low-to-high for the reverse pattern.
regression: Perform with a light band instead of the cable stack.

name: Woodchopper (Cable, Low to High)
equipment: Cable machine, low pulley, rope or handle
steps: Stand side-on to a low pulley, holding the handle with both hands near the outside hip.
Rotate and pull the handle diagonally up and across to above the opposite shoulder.
Let the back foot pivot naturally with the hip rotation.
Return under control along the same path.
mistakes: Isolating the arms and skipping hip rotation.
Hyperextending the lower back to add height.
tips: Mirrors an uppercut or an underarm throw — valuable for many field-sport athletes.
Keep the movement smooth, not jerky.
safety: Keep the load light until the pattern is grooved.
progression: Add load, or increase speed for a power emphasis.
regression: Perform with a resistance band.

name: Farmer's Walk March
steps: Hold a moderate dumbbell in each hand, standing tall.
Brace the core and march in place, lifting the knees to hip height.
Keep the torso vertical and the dumbbells still — no swinging.
March for the prescribed time or step count.
mistakes: Leaning back to counterbalance the load.
Letting the dumbbells swing forward and back.
Rushing the march and losing knee height.
tips: A stationary variation of the farmer's carry that emphasises anti-flexion and hip flexor endurance.
Useful where walking space is limited.
safety: Choose a weight that does not pull the shoulders forward.
progression: Add load, or march with a high-knee emphasis.
regression: March without weights.

name: V-Up
steps: Lie flat, arms extended overhead, legs straight.
Simultaneously lift the torso and legs, reaching the hands toward the toes.
Form a V-shape at the top, balancing briefly on the sit bones.
Lower both halves together under control.
mistakes: Using momentum by throwing the arms and legs up.
Bending the knees to make it easier without acknowledging the regression.
Only lifting the torso and barely raising the legs.
tips: A demanding, whole-abdomen movement — most beginners should regress rather than force it.
If the lower back arches during the lift, the load or range is too much.
safety: Keep the movement slow and controlled, not thrown.
progression: Add a medicine ball held between the hands.
regression: Bent-knee V-up (tuck-up), lifting the knees toward the chest instead.

name: Stability Ball Rollout
steps: Kneel behind a stability ball with the forearms resting on top.
Brace the core, then roll the ball forward by extending the arms and hips together.
Stop before the lower back arches, keeping a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Pull back to the start using the abdominals.
breathing: Inhale rolling out, exhale pulling back.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag as the ball rolls forward.
Rolling out further than strength allows.
Using the ball's momentum instead of controlled muscular effort.
tips: A gentler alternative to the ab wheel with a larger, more forgiving base of support.
Excellent bridge exercise between planks and a full ab-wheel rollout.
safety: Use a ball rated for your bodyweight.
progression: Increase the rollout distance; then move to an ab wheel.
regression: Reduce the rollout range.

name: Weighted Sit-Up
equipment: Bodyweight, or a plate held at the chest
steps: Lie on the back, knees bent, feet anchored or flat on the floor.
Hold a plate across the chest for added resistance if progressing.
Curl the spine up to a full sit-up, leading with the chest.
Lower under control through the full range.
mistakes: Yanking the body up using momentum.
Anchoring the feet so hip flexors dominate entirely over the abs.
Adding load before bodyweight sit-ups are controlled.
tips: Sit-ups load the hip flexors more than crunches — useful for some goals, less ideal for others with anterior pelvic tilt or lower back issues.
Choose crunch variations instead if lower back discomfort appears.
safety: Do not add load if you experience any lower back pain during the movement.
avoid: Anterior pelvic tilt with associated pain
progression: Add a weight plate progressively.
regression: Standard bodyweight crunch with a smaller range.

name: Side Bend (Dumbbell)
steps: Stand tall holding one dumbbell at the side, other hand on the hip or behind the head.
Keep the torso facing forward — no twisting.
Bend directly sideways toward the weighted side as far as comfortable.
Return to upright, then continue past neutral slightly to the opposite side if desired.
breathing: Exhale returning to centre, inhale bending.
mistakes: Twisting the torso instead of bending purely sideways.
Using very heavy weight, which risks the lumbar spine.
Rushing through the range.
tips: Keep this light. Heavy weighted side bends are one of the few exercises with a genuinely poor risk-to-reward ratio for the spine.
Most people get more value from a Pallof press or suitcase carry than from this movement.
safety: Prioritise anti-rotation and anti-lateral-flexion carries over heavy weighted side bends.
progression: Very slight load increase only.
regression: Bodyweight side bend, hand sliding down the thigh.

name: Burpee
steps: Start standing, then squat down and place both hands on the floor.
Jump or step the feet back into a plank position.
Perform one push-up (or lower the chest to the floor).
Jump the feet back to the hands, then explode upward into a jump with arms overhead.
breathing: Exhale on the jump, breathe rhythmically throughout.
mistakes: Letting the lower back sag in the plank phase.
Skipping the push-up depth to move faster.
Landing the jump with locked, stiff knees.
tips: Step back instead of jumping back to reduce impact while keeping the pattern intact.
This is a technique drill first, a conditioning tool second — sloppy burpees teach poor patterns fast.
safety: Land softly with bent knees.
Regress to a step-back burpee if wrist or shoulder pain appears.
progression: Add a tuck jump at the top, or a push-up clap.
regression: Step-back burpee without the push-up or the jump.

name: Kettlebell Swing (Russian)
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, kettlebell on the floor a foot in front.
Hinge and grip the handle, shoulders slightly ahead of the bell.
Hike the bell back between the legs, then explosively extend the hips forward.
Let the arms float to roughly chest/shoulder height — driven by hip power, not arm lifting.
Let the bell fall back into the next hike as the hips re-load.
breathing: Sharp exhale on the hip snap, inhale as the bell swings back.
mistakes: Squatting the swing instead of hinging — this is a hip-hinge exercise, not a squat.
Using the arms and shoulders to lift the bell.
Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the swing.
tips: The hips snap; the arms are just along for the ride.
Think of the top position as a standing plank, not a lean-back.
The single best hip-power teaching tool in the entire database.
safety: Learn the hip hinge with a dowel before adding the kettlebell.
Never let the bell rise above chest height under momentum you cannot control.
progression: Add load, or progress to the American (overhead) swing.
regression: Two-hand hip hinge drill without a bell, or a lighter kettlebell.

name: Kettlebell Goblet Carry
steps: Hold the kettlebell by the horns at chest height, elbows tucked.
Stand tall with the ribcage stacked over the pelvis.
Walk at a controlled pace, keeping the kettlebell still against the chest.
Set it down under control at the end of the distance.
mistakes: Letting the elbows flare out.
Leaning back to counterbalance the load.
tips: An accessible carry variation for anyone new to loaded carries.
Doubles as anti-flexion core training, since the load sits in front of the torso.
safety: Choose a weight that does not force the torso to lean back.
progression: Add load or distance.
regression: Shorter distance, lighter load.

name: Turkish Get-Up
secondary: Stabilising muscles throughout the kinetic chain
steps: Lie on the back holding a light weight overhead with a locked arm; bend the same-side knee.
Roll onto the opposite forearm, then press up to the opposite hand.
Lift the hips high, sweep the straight leg back, and drop to a kneeling lunge.
Stand up out of the lunge, keeping the arm locked overhead throughout.
Reverse the entire sequence with control to return to the floor.
breathing: Breathe steadily; never rush a rep.
mistakes: Losing sight of the weight — the eyes should track it for most of the movement.
Rushing between positions.
Letting the locked arm bend or waver.
tips: Learn each of the 6-7 positions separately before linking them.
One of the best full-body integration and shoulder-stability drills that exists.
Start with no load at all — a shoe balanced on the fist works well.
safety: Practice on a soft surface while learning.
Never rush the transitions.
progression: Add load progressively; this movement rewards patience over years, not weeks.
regression: Half get-up (floor to elbow-support only).

name: TRX Row
steps: Anchor the straps overhead and lean back, holding the handles with straight arms.
Set feet together, body in a straight line — the more horizontal the lean, the harder the row.
Pull the chest to the hands, driving the elbows back.
Lower under control to full arm extension.
mistakes: Piking at the hips instead of keeping a straight body line.
Using a small, partial range.
Letting the shoulders roll forward at the bottom.
tips: Walk the feet forward to make it easier, back to make it harder — instant self-regulated loading.
Fantastic option for hostel rooms and travel with a door anchor.
safety: Check the anchor point rating before every set.
progression: Walk the feet back for a steeper, harder angle.
regression: Walk the feet forward toward the anchor.

name: Battle Rope Wave (Alternating)
steps: Anchor the ropes and hold one end in each hand, feet shoulder-width, knees soft.
Sit into a quarter-squat and brace the core.
Whip the arms alternately up and down, driving waves down the length of the rope.
Maintain a consistent rhythm for the prescribed interval.
breathing: Breathe hard and rhythmically — this is a genuine conditioning tool.
mistakes: Standing bolt upright and using only the shoulders.
Letting the core relax, which loads the lower back.
Going all-out for so long that wave quality collapses in the first 10 seconds.
tips: Bend the knees and engage the legs — the power comes from the whole body, not the arms alone.
Short, intense intervals (20-30 s) beat long, sloppy ones.
safety: Keep a firm, dry grip on the ropes.
progression: Increase interval duration, or use double waves.
regression: Slower tempo, shorter interval.

name: Medicine Ball Slam
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, ball held overhead with both hands.
Brace the core and hinge slightly as you begin the downward motion.
Slam the ball forcefully into the floor between the feet.
Catch the bounce (or pick it back up) and reset for the next rep.
breathing: Exhale sharply on the slam, inhale on the reset.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back on the downswing.
Using only the arms without hip drive.
Standing too close and hitting the shins with the rebound.
tips: A superb stress-relief and power exercise in one movement.
Keep reps low and intent high — this is a power drill, not an endurance one.
safety: Use a genuine non-bounce slam ball, never a regular medicine ball, on hard floors.
progression: Heavier ball, or add a jump before each slam.
regression: Lighter ball, controlled tempo.

name: Jump Squat
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, hands at the chest or swinging freely.
Descend into a quarter-to-half squat.
Explode upward, leaving the ground fully, reaching for maximum height.
Land softly with bent knees, absorbing the impact before the next rep.
breathing: Exhale on the jump, inhale on the landing reset.
mistakes: Landing with stiff, locked knees.
Letting the knees cave inward on landing.
Chaining reps so fast that landing quality suffers.
tips: The landing is the exercise. A loud landing is a warning sign, not a badge of effort.
Rest fully between sets — this is a power exercise, not a conditioning one.
safety: Perform on a surface with some give — never on concrete.
Stop the set if landing mechanics degrade.
progression: Add a tuck to the jump, or progress to box jumps.
regression: Bodyweight squat with a calf raise at the top instead of a full jump.

name: Plyometric Box Jump
steps: Stand facing a stable box roughly shin-to-knee height, feet shoulder-width.
Load the hips back and swing the arms down.
Explode upward and forward, landing softly on the box with knees slightly bent.
Stand fully upright on the box, then step down — never jump backwards off it.
mistakes: Choosing a box height that only works with knee tuck, not true hip extension.
Jumping down off the box, which stresses the joints unnecessarily.
Chasing height once landing mechanics start to break down.
tips: Step down, always. Jumping down is where most box jump injuries happen.
Master the standing broad jump landing before adding box height.
safety: Use a box with a soft or non-slip top.
Ensure adequate space and lighting.
avoid: Any lower limb injury history without clearance
progression: Increase box height only while landing mechanics remain clean.
regression: Step-up performed explosively instead of a full jump.

name: Broad Jump
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, arms ready to swing.
Load the hips back, swing the arms behind you.
Explode forward and upward, extending the hips fully in the air.
Land softly with bent knees, sticking the landing before resetting.
mistakes: Under-using the arm swing.
Landing stiff-legged.
Chaining jumps without resetting between reps.
tips: A true measure of horizontal power output and a foundational athletic drill.
Distance is a bonus; a controlled, silent landing is the actual goal.
safety: Use a surface with grip and some give.
progression: Chain into consecutive broad jumps once single-jump landings are clean.
regression: Standing long step instead of a full jump.

name: High Knees
steps: Stand tall and begin jogging in place.
Drive each knee up to hip height in rapid succession.
Pump the arms in opposition to the legs.
Stay on the balls of the feet throughout.
mistakes: Leaning back, which reduces knee height and stresses the lower back.
Slapping the feet down loudly instead of landing softly.
tips: A staple warm-up and HIIT filler — cheap on joints, high on heart rate.
Keep the torso tall throughout.
safety: Land on the balls of the feet, not the heels.
progression: Increase speed or duration.
regression: Marching in place at a slower tempo.

name: Jump Rope
steps: Hold the rope handles lightly, elbows close to the ribs.
Rotate the rope primarily from the wrists, not the shoulders.
Jump just high enough to clear the rope — a few centimetres.
Land softly on the balls of the feet with slightly bent knees.
mistakes: Jumping too high, which wastes energy and increases impact.
Rotating from the shoulders instead of the wrists.
Landing flat-footed.
tips: The most time-efficient cardio tool that exists — genuinely comparable to running for calorie cost.
Start with short 20-30 second intervals if new to it; the calf demand is significant.
safety: Use a surface with some give.
Wear supportive footwear.
progression: Add double-unders or single-leg skips.
regression: Perform the arm and jump pattern without a rope (imaginary rope).

name: Sled Push
steps: Set the hands on the sled poles at chest to shoulder height.
Lean into the sled with a long body line, arms mostly extended.
Drive through the legs in strong, deliberate steps, staying low.
Maintain the push for the prescribed distance.
mistakes: Standing too upright, which turns it into an arm push.
Taking short, choppy steps.
Rounding the upper back.
tips: An almost injury-proof way to build leg strength and conditioning simultaneously — no eccentric loading.
Excellent choice for anyone returning from a lower-body injury under guidance.
safety: Keep the push area clear of obstacles.
Wear shoes with good traction.
avoid: Acute knee injury (light loads may be appropriate; consult a professional)
progression: Add load, or increase distance.
regression: Reduce load significantly, shorten distance.

name: Bear Crawl
steps: Start on hands and feet, knees hovering a few centimetres off the floor.
Keep the back flat and the hips roughly level with the shoulders.
Crawl forward, moving the opposite hand and foot together.
Keep the knees low and the movement controlled throughout.
mistakes: Letting the hips pike up high.
Moving the same-side hand and foot together (a loss of contralateral pattern).
Letting the knees drag or bang the floor.
tips: A genuinely excellent whole-body stability and coordination drill, popular in youth and rehab settings alike.
Keep the movements small and controlled rather than fast.
safety: Use knee pads on hard floors if the knees are sensitive.
progression: Add lateral or backward bear crawls.
regression: Crawl with the knees resting down between steps.

name: Renegade Row
steps: Start in a push-up plank, one hand on each dumbbell, feet wide for stability.
Brace hard to keep the hips square and still.
Row one dumbbell to the hip, keeping the torso from rotating.
Lower with control, then repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Letting the hips rotate toward the lifted side.
Widening the feet so much that the row loses its anti-rotation challenge.
Using dumbbells that are too heavy to control the rotation.
tips: If the hips rock, the weight is too heavy — the anti-rotation is the point, not the row itself.
Use hex dumbbells so they do not roll.
safety: Keep the wrists neutral and stacked directly under the shoulders throughout.
progression: Add a push-up between rows.
regression: Perform from the knees.

name: Devil's Press
steps: Start standing with a dumbbell in each hand.
Place the dumbbells down and perform a burpee, hands on the dumbbells.
From the plank, jump the feet forward to the hands.
Stand and perform a double dumbbell swing/clean into an overhead press in one fluid motion.
breathing: Exhale on the press, breathe rhythmically overall.
mistakes: Rounding the back on the swing-up phase.
Sacrificing the plank position in the burpee portion.
Using weight too heavy for the overhead component.
tips: One of the most demanding conditioning exercises in strength sport — start with very light dumbbells.
Master the burpee and the dumbbell swing separately before combining them.
safety: Not a beginner exercise.
Requires a solid burpee and overhead pressing base first.
progression: Increase load, or increase reps per round in a HIIT format.
regression: Separate the burpee and the dumbbell swing-press into two distinct movements.

name: Wall Ball
steps: Hold a medicine ball at chest height, feet shoulder-width, facing a wall.
Squat down to at least parallel.
Drive up explosively, extending the legs and throwing the ball to a target on the wall.
Catch the ball on the way down and immediately absorb it into the next squat.
breathing: Exhale on the throw, inhale on the catch.
mistakes: Using the arms only, without leg drive.
Squatting too shallow to build power.
Losing the catch and letting the ball drop uncontrolled.
tips: The legs generate the power; the arms just guide the ball.
A superb combined strength-conditioning tool for time-crunched sessions.
safety: Use a target height appropriate to ceiling clearance.
Clear the throwing area.
progression: Heavier ball, higher target, or shorten rest.
regression: Goblet squat with a light medicine ball, no throw.

name: Low-Impact Step Touch
steps: Stand tall with feet together, arms relaxed.
Step the right foot out to the side, then tap the left foot to meet it.
Step the left foot back out, tapping the right foot to meet it.
Add a gentle arm swing to increase the cardio demand.
mistakes: Bouncing so hard it becomes a joint-jarring movement rather than low-impact.
Locking the knees at the top of each step.
tips: The default choice for joint pain, pregnancy, obesity, or true beginners who need cardio without impact.
Add arm patterns to raise heart rate without adding impact.
safety: Keep a soft bend in the knees throughout.
avoid: None significant — this is one of the safest cardio options available
progression: Add larger steps or arm overhead reaches.
regression: Reduce the range of the side step.

name: Shadow Boxing
steps: Adopt a boxing stance, one foot slightly forward, hands guarding the face.
Throw controlled jabs, crosses, and hooks into open air.
Keep the feet moving — small steps, pivots, and weight shifts.
Maintain a steady rhythm and breathe out sharply on each punch.
mistakes: Locking the elbows on every punch (hyperextension risk over time).
Standing flat-footed with no footwork.
Holding the breath during combinations.
tips: A genuinely enjoyable cardio option that also builds coordination and rotational power.
Snap the punches back rather than pushing them out and leaving them extended.
safety: Keep the wrists straight even without gloves.
progression: Add light dumbbells (under 1 kg) or increase round duration.
regression: Slower tempo, shorter rounds.

name: Office Chair Squat
steps: Stand in front of a sturdy chair, feet shoulder-width.
Push the hips back and lower until the glutes lightly touch the seat.
Do not sit down fully — pause briefly, then drive back up to standing.
Keep the chest tall throughout.
mistakes: Fully collapsing into the seat and resting between reps.
Letting the knees track far past the toes.
Using a chair with wheels.
tips: A discreet way to break up sedentary desk time without needing a change of clothes.
Can be done in work attire, in a meeting-adjacent room, or between calls.
safety: Confirm the chair is stable and cannot roll or tip.
progression: Remove the chair touch and go to a full bodyweight squat.
regression: Sit fully and stand using the hands for assistance.

name: Suitcase Step-Up (Loaded Carry + Step)
equipment: One dumbbell or kettlebell, box or step
steps: Hold one weight at the side in a suitcase-carry grip.
Step up onto a box with the opposite leg to the loaded hand.
Stand tall on the box without letting the torso lean toward the weight.
Step down with control and repeat, then switch sides.
breathing: Exhale stepping up, inhale stepping down.
mistakes: Leaning toward the loaded side.
Using momentum instead of a controlled step.
tips: Combines two evidence-backed patterns — the unilateral step-up and the anti-lateral-flexion carry — into one efficient drill.
Popular in athletic and tactical conditioning programs.
safety: Confirm the box is stable before loading it.
progression: Add load, or raise the box height.
regression: Bodyweight step-up without the carry.

name: Partner Med Ball Rotational Throw
steps: Stand side-on to your partner, roughly 2-3 m apart, holding the ball at the hip.
Load by rotating the torso and hips away from the partner.
Explosively rotate and release the ball toward the partner's chest height.
Catch the return throw and immediately load into the next rep.
breathing: Exhale on the throw, inhale on the catch.
mistakes: Throwing with arms only, no hip rotation.
Standing too close, removing the value of the rotational range.
Using a ball too heavy to control safely.
tips: Mirrors rotational sport actions like a cricket throw or a golf swing far better than a machine ever could.
Communicate clearly with your partner before every throw.
safety: Use a soft-shell medicine ball for catching safety.
Ensure adequate space free of obstacles.
progression: Increase ball weight or throw distance.
regression: Throw against a wall solo instead of with a partner.

name: Resistance Band Squat to Row
steps: Anchor a band at chest height and face it, holding a handle in each hand.
Step back for tension, then squat down with arms extended toward the anchor.
Stand up while simultaneously rowing the handles to the ribs.
Reverse smoothly back into the next squat.
breathing: Exhale standing and rowing, inhale squatting.
mistakes: Disconnecting the squat and the row into two separate, jerky movements.
Rounding the back during the squat portion.
tips: A genuinely efficient full-body combination move for time-limited home sessions.
Keep the two halves of the movement smoothly linked.
safety: Inspect the band before each session.
avoid: Acute knee or lower back pain
progression: Thicker band, or slow the tempo.
regression: Separate into a bodyweight squat and a band row.

name: Sandbag Carry (Bear Hug)
steps: Hug the sandbag against the chest, wrapping the arms fully around it.
Stand tall, brace the core hard against the awkward, shifting load.
Walk at a controlled pace for the prescribed distance.
Set the bag down with a controlled squat, not a drop.
breathing: Breathe continuously despite the compression on the chest.
mistakes: Letting the lower back round to compensate for the awkward hold.
Rushing the walk and losing control of the shifting sand.
tips: Unstable, shifting loads like sand build a different, highly functional kind of strength than fixed weights.
A duffel bag filled with towels or clothing is a perfectly good substitute.
safety: Lift the bag with a proper hip hinge, not a rounded back.
progression: Add weight, or increase distance.
regression: Lighter bag, shorter distance.

name: Inchworm Walkout
steps: Stand tall, then hinge forward and place the hands on the floor.
Walk the hands forward into a plank, keeping the legs as straight as comfortable.
Hold the plank briefly, then walk the feet toward the hands.
Roll back up to standing one vertebra at a time.
mistakes: Bending the knees excessively to avoid the hamstring stretch.
Sagging the hips during the walkout plank.
Rushing through without pausing in the plank.
tips: A superb dynamic warm-up that combines a hamstring stretch, a plank, and a hip-hinge pattern in one flow.
Bend the knees as much as needed — the walkout, not the straight legs, is the priority.
safety: Warm up gradually rather than forcing the stretch on cold muscles.
progression: Add a push-up at the bottom of the plank.
regression: Bend the knees generously throughout.

name: Olympic Barbell Clean (Power Clean)
steps: Set up as for a deadlift, bar over mid-foot, shins close to the bar.
Pull the bar past the knees while accelerating the hips into full extension.
As the bar reaches hip height, shrug and pull the body under it explosively.
Catch the bar on the front of the shoulders in a quarter-squat, then stand tall.
breathing: Explosive exhale through the pull; breathe and reset between reps.
mistakes: Pulling early with the arms instead of the legs and hips.
Failing to fully extend the hips before pulling under.
Catching with the elbows low, which drops the bar off the shoulders.
tips: This is a technical lift that rewards patience — hire a qualified coach for the first several sessions.
The bar should stay close to the body throughout the entire pull.
safety: Requires dedicated technical coaching before loading.
Do not attempt without prior instruction.
avoid: Any wrist, shoulder, or lower back pathology
progression: Increase load only under qualified coaching once technique is consistent.
regression: Hang high pull or kettlebell swing to build the hip-extension pattern first.

name: Dumbbell Thruster
steps: Hold a dumbbell at each shoulder, feet shoulder-width.
Squat down to at least parallel.
Drive up explosively, using the leg momentum to press the dumbbells overhead in one motion.
Lower the dumbbells back to the shoulders as you descend into the next squat.
breathing: Exhale on the press, inhale on the squat.
mistakes: Pausing between the squat and the press, losing the momentum transfer.
Pressing with the arms alone without leg drive.
Arching the lower back at the top.
tips: The whole point is the seamless transfer of leg power into the press — that link is the skill.
A brutally efficient full-body conditioning tool in a short amount of time.
safety: Use a weight light enough to maintain full-body coordination.
progression: Increase load or reduce rest between sets.
regression: Separate into a goblet squat followed by a shoulder press.

name: Mountain Pose
benefits: Improves posture awareness
Establishes grounding before a sequence
Gently activates the feet and legs
steps: Stand with the feet together or hip-width, weight spread evenly across each foot.
Engage the thighs gently and lengthen the spine upward.
Roll the shoulders back and down, letting the arms rest at the sides.
Draw the chin level and soften the gaze forward.
breathing: Slow, even breaths through the nose; 5-8 breaths.
mistakes: Locking the knees.
Letting the ribcage flare forward.
Tensing the shoulders toward the ears.
progression: Add an overhead reach on the inhale.
regression: Practice against a wall for tactile feedback on alignment.

name: Downward-Facing Dog
benefits: Lengthens the hamstrings and calves
Builds shoulder and upper back strength
Gently decompresses the spine
steps: Start on hands and knees, hands slightly ahead of the shoulders.
Tuck the toes and lift the hips up and back, straightening the legs as much as comfortable.
Press the chest toward the thighs, forming an inverted V shape.
Pedal the feet gently to release the calves.
breathing: Long, even breaths; exhale to deepen the fold slightly.
mistakes: Rounding the upper back sharply.
Locking the knees to force straight legs.
Letting the heels force the movement instead of the hips.
progression: Deepen by walking the hands forward slightly to increase the shoulder stretch.
regression: Bend the knees generously and focus only on lengthening the spine.

name: Child's Pose
benefits: Releases tension in the lower back and hips
Calms the nervous system
Gentle knee and ankle stretch
avoid: Knee injury (widen the knees or avoid)
steps: Kneel with the big toes touching and knees wide.
Sit the hips back toward the heels.
Fold the torso forward, extending the arms ahead or resting them alongside the body.
Rest the forehead on the mat and relax completely.
breathing: Slow diaphragmatic breathing, feeling the ribs expand into the thighs.
mistakes: Holding tension in the shoulders instead of releasing them.
Forcing the hips onto the heels when hip flexibility does not allow it.
progression: Walk the hands further forward for a deeper shoulder stretch.
regression: Place a cushion between the hips and heels for support.

name: Cat-Cow Flow
benefits: Warms up the entire spine
Improves spinal mobility segment by segment
Coordinates breath with movement
avoid: Acute disc herniation with pain on flexion or extension
steps: Start on hands and knees, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips.
Inhale, drop the belly, lift the chest and tailbone (Cow).
Exhale, round the spine toward the ceiling, tucking the chin and tailbone (Cat).
Continue flowing smoothly between the two positions with the breath.
breathing: Inhale into Cow, exhale into Cat.
mistakes: Moving faster than the breath allows.
Initiating from the neck instead of the spine as a whole.
progression: Add a lateral spine wave once the sagittal flow feels smooth.
regression: Perform seated in a chair with hands on the knees.

name: Warrior I
benefits: Strengthens the legs and opens the hip flexors
Builds shoulder stability overhead
Improves balance and focus
avoid: Knee pain in the front leg
steps: From standing, step one foot back about a leg's length, turning it out slightly.
Bend the front knee to roughly 90 degrees, keeping it tracking over the ankle.
Square the hips toward the front of the mat as much as comfortable.
Raise the arms overhead, reaching through the fingertips.
breathing: Steady breathing, lengthening the spine on each inhale.
mistakes: Letting the front knee drift past the toes or collapse inward.
Allowing the back heel to lift when it should stay grounded (or lift purposefully in a modified version).
Overarching the lower back to raise the arms higher.
progression: Deepen the back-leg stretch by lengthening the stance further.
regression: Keep the hands on the hips instead of raising the arms overhead.

name: Warrior II
benefits: Builds lower body strength and stamina
Opens the hips and groin
Develops focus and steady breath under muscular fatigue
steps: Step the feet wide, front foot forward, back foot turned out 90 degrees.
Bend the front knee to a right angle, keeping it over the ankle.
Extend the arms parallel to the floor, gaze over the front hand.
Sink the hips low, keeping the torso upright over the pelvis.
breathing: Steady, even breathing; avoid breath-holding despite the burn.
mistakes: Leaning the torso over the front thigh.
Letting the front knee cave inward.
Raising the shoulders toward the ears.
progression: Hold longer, or transition into a reverse warrior for added range.
regression: Shorten the stance and reduce the knee bend depth.

name: Triangle Pose
benefits: Stretches the hamstrings, hips, and side body
Strengthens the legs
Improves spinal rotation and lateral flexibility
steps: Step the feet wide, front foot forward, back foot turned in slightly.
Extend the arms parallel to the floor, then hinge at the front hip.
Lower the front hand to the shin, ankle, or a block, extending the top arm skyward.
Keep both sides of the torso long — avoid collapsing into the front hip.
breathing: Steady breathing, using the exhale to lengthen slightly deeper.
mistakes: Collapsing the torso forward instead of extending long and hinging sideways.
Locking the front knee aggressively.
Turning the head to look up before the neck is ready.
progression: Lower the bottom hand to the floor or a block placed outside the shin.
regression: Rest the bottom hand higher, on the shin instead of the ankle.

name: Tree Pose
benefits: Improves single-leg balance and ankle stability
Strengthens the standing leg and core
Builds focus and calm concentration
conditions: Mild balance concerns (practice near a wall)
steps: Stand tall and shift weight into one foot.
Place the sole of the other foot on the inner calf or inner thigh, avoiding the knee joint.
Bring the hands to the heart or extend them overhead once stable.
Fix the gaze on a single still point to aid balance.
breathing: Slow, even breathing helps steady the balance.
mistakes: Resting the foot directly on the knee joint, which stresses the ligaments.
Gripping the standing-leg toes to compensate for poor balance.
progression: Close the eyes once stable, or move the arms overhead with eyes closed.
regression: Keep the toes of the lifted foot touching the floor for extra support.

name: Chair Pose
benefits: Builds quadriceps and glute endurance
Strengthens the ankles and core
Raises the heart rate mildly
steps: Stand with feet together or hip-width.
Bend the knees and sit the hips back as if sitting into an invisible chair.
Raise the arms overhead, keeping the ribs drawn in.
Keep the weight in the heels, not the toes.
breathing: Steady breathing; resist the urge to hold the breath under the burn.
mistakes: Letting the knees track far past the toes.
Arching the lower back to compensate for the arm raise.
Rising onto the toes.
progression: Lower the hips deeper, or add a heel raise (Chair to Toe Stand).
regression: Reduce the depth of the knee bend and lower the arms to shoulder height.

name: Extended Side Angle
benefits: Stretches the side body and hip flexors
Strengthens the legs
Opens the chest and shoulders
avoid: Knee pain in the front leg
Neck pain (look forward instead of up)
steps: From a wide stance, bend the front knee to a right angle.
Lower the front forearm to the thigh or the front hand to the floor/block.
Extend the top arm overhead in one long diagonal line from the back foot to the fingertips.
Keep the chest rotating open toward the ceiling.
breathing: Long, steady breaths, expanding the ribcage with each inhale.
mistakes: Letting the front knee collapse inward.
Dumping weight onto the front forearm instead of maintaining a long side-body line.
progression: Lower the front hand to the outside of the foot for a deeper bind option.
regression: Rest the forearm on the thigh rather than reaching to the floor.

name: Seated Forward Fold
benefits: Deeply stretches the hamstrings and lower back
Calms the nervous system
Improves spinal flexibility
steps: Sit with the legs extended straight ahead, spine tall.
Inhale to lengthen the spine, exhale to hinge forward from the hips.
Reach for the shins, ankles, or feet — wherever the current range allows.
Relax the neck and let the head hang naturally.
breathing: Slow exhales to deepen the fold gradually over several breaths.
mistakes: Rounding the spine from the top instead of hinging from the hips.
Forcing the reach and bouncing to gain extra range.
Locking the knees painfully straight.
progression: Deepen gradually over weeks; never force a forward fold.
regression: Bend the knees generously and use a strap around the feet.

name: Bound Angle Pose
benefits: Opens the hips and inner thighs
Improves circulation to the pelvic region
Gently stretches the groin
steps: Sit tall and bring the soles of the feet together, knees falling out to the sides.
Hold the feet or ankles with the hands.
Lengthen the spine on the inhale; fold forward slightly on the exhale if comfortable.
Let the knees release toward the floor without forcing them down.
breathing: Slow, even breathing, releasing tension on each exhale.
duration: 30-60 s, or up to 2 minutes for a restorative hold
mistakes: Pressing down on the knees with the hands or elbows.
Rounding the back forcefully to increase the fold.
progression: Fold the torso forward while keeping the spine long.
regression: Place cushions under each knee for support.

name: Head-to-Knee Forward Bend
benefits: Stretches one hamstring and the spine at a time
Calms the mind
Improves hip flexibility asymmetrically
avoid: Knee injury on the bent-leg side
steps: Sit with one leg extended, the other foot drawn in to the inner thigh.
Square the hips toward the extended leg.
Inhale to lengthen, exhale to fold forward over the straight leg.
Hold the shin, ankle, or foot without forcing the reach.
breathing: Slow exhales to ease deeper over several breaths.
mistakes: Letting the hips rotate away from the extended leg.
Rounding aggressively from the upper back.
progression: Deepen gradually; add a slight twist toward the extended leg.
regression: Bend the extended knee slightly and use a strap.

name: Seated Spinal Twist
benefits: Improves spinal rotation and mobility
Stimulates digestion
Relieves tension along the back
steps: Sit tall with one leg extended and the other foot crossed over it, planted near the knee.
Inhale to lengthen the spine.
Exhale and rotate the torso toward the bent knee, using the opposite elbow as gentle leverage.
Look over the back shoulder if the neck allows.
breathing: Inhale to lengthen before each rotation, exhale to twist deeper.
mistakes: Twisting from the lower back instead of rotating the whole spine evenly.
Forcing the twist with the arms rather than leading with the breath.
progression: Deepen the bind by wrapping the arm around the shin.
regression: Keep the bottom leg bent instead of extended.

name: Cobra Pose
benefits: Strengthens the lower back and spinal extensors
Opens the chest
Counteracts hours of forward-flexed posture
steps: Lie face down, hands under the shoulders, elbows tucked close to the ribs.
Press the tops of the feet and pubic bone into the mat.
Inhale and lift the chest, keeping the lower ribs on or near the floor.
Keep the elbows slightly bent — this is not a full push-up.
breathing: Inhale to lift, exhale to hold or release.
mistakes: Using the arms to force the chest too high, which strains the lumbar spine.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears.
Fully straightening the elbows (that is Upward Dog, a different, more advanced pose).
progression: Progress toward Upward-Facing Dog once thoracic mobility improves.
regression: Lift only a few centimetres, keeping most of the weight in the forearms (Sphinx variation).

name: Bridge Pose
benefits: Strengthens the glutes and hamstrings
Opens the chest and hip flexors
Gently stimulates the thyroid region
steps: Lie on the back, knees bent, feet hip-width close to the glutes.
Press into the feet and lift the hips toward the ceiling.
Interlace the hands under the back and press the arms down for lift, or keep them at the sides.
Keep the chin gently tucked, weight even across both feet.
breathing: Inhale to lift, breathe steadily through the hold, exhale to lower.
mistakes: Turning the head side to side while lifted.
Letting the knees splay outward.
Pushing off the neck instead of the feet and arms.
progression: Progress to Wheel Pose only with adequate wrist and shoulder mobility and supervision.
regression: Place a yoga block under the sacrum for a supported, passive version.

name: Locust Pose
benefits: Strengthens the entire posterior chain
Improves postural endurance
Builds spinal extensor strength without arm assistance
steps: Lie face down, arms alongside the body, palms facing down or up.
Inhale and lift the chest, arms, and legs simultaneously off the floor.
Reach long through the fingertips and toes rather than crunching the back.
Hold, then lower with control on the exhale.
breathing: Inhale to lift, hold with steady breathing, exhale to lower.
mistakes: Yanking the head back and craning the neck.
Bending the knees to gain artificial height.
Holding the breath through the entire lift.
progression: Extend the hold duration, or clasp the hands behind the back for a deeper chest opener.
regression: Lift only the chest, keeping the legs on the floor.

name: Sphinx Pose
benefits: Gently opens the chest and lower back
Improves lumbar extension tolerance
Suitable for desk-related stiffness
avoid: Acute lower back pain (case-dependent — start very gently)
steps: Lie face down, forearms on the mat, elbows under the shoulders.
Press the forearms down and lift the chest, keeping the hips and legs relaxed on the mat.
Draw the shoulder blades down the back.
Keep the neck long, gaze forward or slightly down.
breathing: Slow, even breathing throughout the hold.
mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up around the ears.
Overextending the neck by looking too far upward.
progression: Progress to Cobra Pose for a deeper extension.
regression: Reduce the height of the lift, staying very gentle.

name: Camel Pose
benefits: Deeply opens the chest, shoulders, and hip flexors
Improves thoracic extension
Counteracts prolonged sitting
steps: Kneel tall with the hips stacked over the knees, hands on the lower back for support.
Engage the core and lift the chest, arching back gradually.
Reach one hand at a time to the heels only if the back allows without strain.
Lead the movement with the chest, not by cranking the neck back.
breathing: Slow inhales to create space, exhale to release out of the pose.
mistakes: Compressing the neck by dropping the head back forcefully.
Sinking into the lower back instead of lifting through the chest first.
Rushing into the deepest version without building up gradually.
progression: Reach the hands to the heels only once comfortable with hands-on-back version.
regression: Keep the hands on the lower back throughout, a gentler variation.

name: Pigeon Pose
benefits: Deeply opens the hip external rotators and flexors
Relieves tightness from running or cycling
Improves hip range of motion
conditions: Tight hips from running or desk sitting
steps: From a tabletop position, bring one knee forward behind the wrist, shin angled across the mat.
Extend the back leg straight behind, hips squared as much as possible.
Fold forward over the front leg, resting on the forearms or a bolster.
Breathe into any areas of tightness rather than forcing deeper.
breathing: Slow, deep breathing; use exhales to soften into the stretch.
mistakes: Letting the front shin angle create pain in the knee — adjust the angle immediately if so.
Collapsing onto one hip instead of staying relatively square.
progression: Reach for the back foot for a quadriceps stretch addition (Mermaid variation).
regression: Perform a reclined figure-four stretch instead if the floor version irritates the knee.

name: Standing Forward Fold
benefits: Stretches the hamstrings and calves
Calms the nervous system
Gently decompresses the spine
conditions: Mild hypertension (avoid dropping the head suddenly)
steps: Stand tall, then hinge at the hips, folding the torso over the legs.
Let the head and neck hang heavy and relaxed.
Hold opposite elbows, or let the hands rest on the floor or shins.
Bend the knees as much as needed to release the lower back.
breathing: Long exhales to soften deeper into the fold.
mistakes: Locking the knees painfully straight.
Rounding aggressively through the lower back to reach the floor.
progression: Straighten the legs gradually as flexibility improves.
regression: Keep a generous bend in the knees throughout.

name: Legs-Up-The-Wall Pose
benefits: Promotes venous return and reduces leg swelling
Deeply calms the nervous system
Gentle inversion without strain
steps: Sit sideways against a wall, then swing the legs up as you lie back.
Scoot the hips as close to the wall as is comfortable.
Rest the arms out to the sides, palms up.
Close the eyes and relax completely for the duration.
breathing: Slow, natural breathing; let it settle on its own.
mistakes: Placing the hips too far from the wall, creating strain rather than rest.
Keeping the shoulders tense instead of letting them melt into the floor.
progression: Add a folded blanket under the hips for a gentle deeper angle.
regression: Bend the knees and rest the calves on a chair seat instead of a wall.

name: Corpse Pose
benefits: Facilitates complete physical and mental relaxation
Consolidates the benefits of the preceding practice
Lowers heart rate and stress markers
avoid: None — modify support if lower back discomfort arises when lying flat
steps: Lie flat on the back, legs relaxed and slightly apart, arms at the sides, palms up.
Close the eyes and allow the whole body to become heavy.
Release any effort in the face, jaw, and hands.
Let the breath return to its natural, unforced rhythm.
breathing: No specific pattern — natural, unforced breathing.
mistakes: Falling fully asleep when the intent is meditative rest (fine occasionally, just note it).
Holding subtle tension in the forehead or jaw.
progression: Extend the duration for a deeper restorative session.
regression: Place a rolled blanket under the knees to release lower back tension.

name: Half Lord of the Fishes
benefits: Improves spinal rotation
Stretches the outer hip and shoulders
Stimulates abdominal organs
steps: Sit tall, bend one knee and step the foot over the opposite thigh.
Bend the other leg, foot near the hip, or extend it straight.
Inhale to lengthen the spine, exhale to rotate toward the bent knee.
Use the opposite arm as a gentle lever against the outer knee.
breathing: Inhale to lengthen, exhale to deepen the twist.
mistakes: Forcing the twist with the arm rather than initiating from the spine.
Rounding the lower back during the rotation.
progression: Bind the arm fully around the shin for a deeper variation.
regression: Keep the bottom leg straight rather than bent underneath.

name: Reclined Bound Angle Pose
benefits: Passive hip and groin opener
Deeply relaxing for the nervous system
Gentle support for menstrual discomfort
steps: Lie on the back and bring the soles of the feet together, knees falling open.
Support each knee with a cushion or block if the hips are tight.
Rest the arms out to the sides, palms up.
Close the eyes and breathe slowly, allowing the hips to release with each exhale.
mistakes: Forcing the knees down toward the floor.
Holding tension in the jaw or shoulders instead of relaxing fully.
progression: Remove the knee supports as hip flexibility improves.
regression: Increase the cushion height under the knees for more support.

name: Standing Forward Fold with Shoulder Opener
benefits: Combines a hamstring stretch with a shoulder and chest opener
Relieves upper back and shoulder tension
steps: Stand and interlace the hands behind the back, straightening the arms.
Hinge forward at the hips, folding the torso over the legs.
Let the arms fall forward over the head, opening the chest and shoulders.
Keep a soft bend in the knees throughout.
breathing: Long exhales to deepen both the fold and the shoulder stretch.
mistakes: Locking the elbows painfully straight.
Rounding the upper back instead of hinging cleanly at the hips.
progression: Deepen the fold as the hamstrings and shoulders both loosen.
regression: Hold a strap between the hands instead of interlacing the fingers.

name: Easy Pose with Forward Fold
benefits: Gently stretches the hips and lower back
Calms the mind for meditation preparation
steps: Sit cross-legged with a tall, relaxed spine.
Inhale to lengthen upward.
Exhale and fold the torso forward over the crossed legs, walking the hands out.
Let the forehead rest toward the floor or a cushion.
breathing: Slow, calming breaths, longer on the exhale.
mistakes: Rounding the back sharply instead of hinging from the hips.
Forcing the fold deeper than current hip flexibility allows.
progression: Hold the fold longer, or walk the hands further out.
regression: Sit on a cushion to elevate the hips above the knees.

name: Standing Side Stretch (Yoga)
benefits: Stretches the entire side body and intercostal muscles
Improves lateral spinal mobility
steps: Stand tall, interlace the fingers, and extend the arms overhead.
Keep both feet grounded and hips facing forward.
Lean the torso to one side, keeping length through the spine — avoid collapsing.
Return to centre and repeat on the other side.
breathing: Inhale to lengthen, exhale to deepen the side bend.
mistakes: Leaning forward instead of purely sideways.
Collapsing the ribcage on the stretched side.
progression: Add a slight backward lean for a deeper oblique stretch.
regression: Keep the hands on the hips instead of overhead.

name: Thread the Needle
benefits: Releases tension in the shoulders and upper back
Gently stretches the thoracic spine in rotation
steps: Start on hands and knees.
Slide the right arm underneath the body, palm up, resting the shoulder and head on the mat.
Keep the left hand planted for support, or extend it overhead.
Breathe into the stretch across the upper back and shoulder.
breathing: Slow, deep breathing, releasing more with each exhale.
mistakes: Collapsing all the weight onto the neck instead of the shoulder.
Rushing out of the pose instead of releasing gradually.
progression: Walk the supporting hand further forward for a deeper stretch.
regression: Place a cushion under the resting shoulder and head.

name: Happy Baby Pose
benefits: Gently opens the hips and inner groin
Releases tension in the lower back
Calming and grounding
steps: Lie on the back and draw the knees toward the chest.
Grip the outside edges of the feet, opening the knees toward the armpits.
Gently rock side to side if it feels good, or hold still.
Keep the lower back relaxed against the mat.
mistakes: Forcing the knees down toward the floor with strain.
Holding the breath instead of breathing into the stretch.
progression: Straighten the legs slightly for a deeper hamstring component.
regression: Hold behind the thighs instead of the feet if flexibility is limited.

name: Neck Side Flexion Stretch
steps: Sit or stand tall, spine long.
Drop the right ear toward the right shoulder without lifting the shoulder.
Rest the right hand gently on the head for light overpressure if desired.
Hold, then switch sides.
cues: Keep the shoulder pinned down throughout.
Move into the stretch slowly, never jerk.
mistakes: Pulling the head down forcefully.
Lifting the opposite shoulder to compensate.
avoid: Discontinue with any radiating pain, numbness or tingling into the arm.
progression: Add gentle overpressure with the hand.
regression: Perform without hand-assisted overpressure.

name: Neck Rotation Stretch
steps: Sit or stand tall.
Slowly turn the head to look over the right shoulder.
Hold at the comfortable end range without forcing.
Return to centre and repeat left.
cues: Keep the shoulders level and still.
Move slowly and stop at the first resistance barrier.
mistakes: Jerking into the rotation.
Rotating the whole torso instead of just the neck.
avoid: Stop with any dizziness, numbness, or sharp pain.
progression: Add a light hand-assisted overpressure at the end range.
regression: Reduce the rotation range.

name: Upper Trapezius Stretch
steps: Sit tall and reach the right hand behind the back or hold the chair seat.
Tilt the head to the left, then gently rotate the chin slightly downward.
Use the left hand for light overpressure if comfortable.
Hold, then switch sides.
cues: Keep the shoulder anchored down by holding the chair or reaching back.
Increase pressure gradually, never suddenly.
mistakes: Yanking the head with the hand.
Shrugging the opposite shoulder.
avoid: Discontinue with radiating symptoms into the arm.
progression: Hold longer, or add the chin-tuck angle for a deeper stretch.
regression: Perform without hand overpressure.

name: Cross-Body Shoulder Stretch
steps: Bring the right arm straight across the chest.
Use the left forearm to gently pull the right arm closer.
Keep the right shoulder down, away from the ear.
Hold, then switch sides.
cues: Anchor the working shoulder down throughout.
Pull from the upper arm, not the wrist.
mistakes: Shrugging the working shoulder up.
Rotating the torso instead of isolating the shoulder.
progression: Deepen the pull gradually over several breaths.
regression: Reduce the pull intensity.

name: Overhead Triceps and Shoulder Stretch
steps: Raise the right arm overhead and bend the elbow, hand falling behind the head.
Use the left hand to gently press the right elbow further back.
Keep the ribcage from flaring forward.
Hold, then switch sides.
cues: Keep the core braced to avoid an exaggerated lower back arch.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to compensate.
Forcing the elbow past a comfortable range.
progression: Add a slight side bend for an additional lat stretch.
regression: Hold the upper arm without bending the elbow fully.

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
steps: Stand in a doorway, forearm against the frame, elbow at shoulder height.
Step forward gently through the doorway until a stretch is felt across the chest.
Keep the torso upright — do not let the shoulder hike up.
Hold, then switch sides.
breathing: Slow, deep breaths into the chest.
cues: Keep the shoulder blade drawn down, not shrugged.
Step forward slowly, in small increments.
mistakes: Stepping too far forward too fast.
Twisting the torso instead of stepping straight through.
progression: Raise or lower the arm position to target different chest fibres.
regression: Reduce the step distance.
