There is no need to actually 'clear the mind' — the forest imagery is simply somewhere pleasant for attention to rest instead.
progression: Extend the walk to a full imagined loop, including arriving somewhere restful like a clearing or viewpoint.
regression: Focus on just one sense (sound of birds, or the feel of a breeze) rather than the whole scene.

name: Beach Meditation
breathing: Slow breathing paced to imagined waves
steps: Sit or lie comfortably and close the eyes.
Picture sitting on a quiet shoreline, the sand warm beneath you.
Imagine each wave rolling in and receding, and let each inhale match the wave's arrival, each exhale its retreat.
Notice the imagined warmth of the sun and the sound of the sea as anchors whenever attention drifts.
focus: The rhythm of imagined waves, paired with breath.
benefits: Pairing breath with an imagined rhythmic pattern (waves) makes the anchor easier to hold onto than breath alone
The associative calm of beach imagery is broadly culturally familiar, making it accessible to most beginners
Doubles well as a pre-sleep practice due to its slow, rhythmic pacing
science: Rhythmic guided imagery combined with breath pacing is a common technique in clinical relaxation training.
mistakes: Letting the imagined scene turn into an elaborate story (a memory of an actual holiday) instead of staying with the present-moment sensory focus.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend into a body scan while remaining in the beach scene, feeling the sand supporting each part of the body.
regression: Focus only on the sound of the waves without building the full visual scene.

name: Mountain Meditation
steps: Sit tall, as if the spine were the peak of a mountain — stable and unmoving.
Imagine standing at a mountain summit, cool fresh air, wide open silence around you.
Notice the stillness and permanence of the mountain, unmoved regardless of weather or clouds passing.
Let this sense of steady, grounded stability settle into the body as you continue breathing.
focus: The felt sense of stillness and stability, mirrored by an upright, grounded seated posture.
benefits: The 'mountain' metaphor is widely used to build a felt sense of stability that carries beyond the practice itself
Pairs a physical posture cue (tall spine) with the mental image for a stronger anchor
Useful before situations that call for calm steadiness, such as a difficult conversation or public speaking
science: Metaphor-based imagery that links posture to a psychological quality (stability, groundedness) is a well-established technique in mindfulness-based approaches.
mistakes: Slouching while trying to feel 'grounded' — the tall, stable posture is part of the practice, not incidental.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Add an intention to carry the mountain's steadiness into a specific upcoming situation.
regression: Shorten to simply sitting tall and breathing, without the extended visualization.

name: Night Sky Meditation
steps: Lie down comfortably and close the eyes.
Imagine lying beneath a clear night sky, stars scattered overhead.
Let the breath slow, imagining each exhale as a star settling gently into place.
Rest in the vastness and quiet of the imagined sky until sleep arrives or the timer ends.
focus: The imagined vastness and stillness of a starlit sky, paired with slowing breath.
benefits: The imagery of vastness has a documented calming effect, sometimes called 'awe-based' relaxation
The slow pacing and lying position make this especially suited to pre-sleep use
Requires no counting or technique — purely restful attention
science: Awe-inducing imagery, including expansive natural scenes like a night sky, has been linked in research to reduced self-focused stress and improved mood.
mistakes: Using a bright screen or phone immediately before or during this practice, which undermines the sleep benefit.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend the practice for as long as needed until sleep arrives naturally.
regression: Focus on just a few imagined stars rather than the whole sky.

name: Positive Memory Focus
steps: Sit comfortably and bring to mind one memory that genuinely makes you happy.
Rather than replaying the whole story, focus only on the core emotion it carries.
Notice where that feeling shows up in the body — warmth, lightness, a natural smile.
Whenever attention wanders, gently guide it back to that single feeling, not the story.
focus: The core felt emotion of one chosen memory, not its narrative detail.
benefits: Deliberately narrowing focus to feeling rather than story prevents rumination on memory details
A genuinely simple, low-barrier entry point to positive-focus meditation
Can be practiced anywhere in under 5 minutes if time is short
science: Positive affect recall is linked in psychological research to short-term mood improvement and reduced stress reactivity.
mistakes: Getting drawn into narrating or analysing the memory instead of resting in the feeling.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Layer in a second happy memory once the first feeling is well established.
regression: Focus on a smaller, everyday positive moment if a big memory feels hard to access.

name: Gratitude Circle Reset
steps: Sit comfortably and bring to mind someone you're grateful for — a parent, friend, teacher, mentor, or even a pet.
Picture their face and silently acknowledge one specific thing they've given or taught you.
Let the feeling of gratitude settle for a few breaths before moving to the next person.
Move through 3-4 people this way, finishing with a moment of gratitude directed at yourself.
focus: The specific felt sense of gratitude toward each person brought to mind, one at a time.
benefits: Regular gratitude practice is one of the most consistently evidenced tools for improving mood and life satisfaction
Structuring it as a sequence of specific people (rather than a vague list) deepens the emotional impact
Naturally counters the mind's negativity bias by deliberately directing attention toward what is good
science: Gratitude interventions have a substantial evidence base in positive psychology research linking them to improved wellbeing and reduced depressive symptoms.
mistakes: Rushing through the list without pausing to actually feel gratitude for each person.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend the circle to include a more difficult relationship, finding one genuine point of gratitude.
regression: Focus on just one person for the full session, going deeper rather than broader.

name: Future Self Visualization
steps: Sit comfortably and bring to mind your healthiest, most capable future self.
Picture how that version of you moves, stands, and feels in the body — energised, capable, at ease.
Imagine a specific everyday moment as that person — waking up, exercising, or simply feeling confident.
Notice the emotions this brings up, and let them motivate the intention for today's actions.
focus: A specific, sensory-detailed everyday moment as the imagined future self.
benefits: Concrete, everyday imagery is a more effective motivator than abstract 'goal' thinking alone
Connecting the vision to feeling (not just appearance) builds more durable motivation
Works well as a weekly practice rather than daily, to avoid the image losing its emotional charge
science: Goal-directed visualization combined with implementation intentions is supported in behavioural psychology as a technique that improves follow-through on health goals.
mistakes: Focusing purely on physical appearance rather than capability and feeling.
Using the practice to criticise the present self by comparison — the aim is inspiration, not judgment.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Pair the visualization with writing down one concrete action for today that moves toward that vision.
regression: Focus on a single specific quality (energy, confidence) rather than a full scene.

name: Workout Visualization
steps: Sit or stand quietly before training begins.
Picture today's workout from start to finish, seeing each exercise performed with perfect form.
Imagine the feeling of strength and control in the body during the hardest set.
Finish by picturing the satisfaction of completing the session as planned.
focus: The specific movements of today's session, rehearsed with correct form and a confident mindset.
benefits: Pre-training mental rehearsal is linked to improved movement quality and reduced hesitation on challenging lifts
Builds a confident mindset before the physical session begins
Short enough to use as a genuine part of the warm-up routine, not a separate task
science: Motor imagery rehearsal before physical training is supported in sport science literature for improving subsequent movement execution and confidence.
mistakes: Visualizing a workout that is unrealistic for today's actual energy and readiness level.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend to visualizing the full session including a plan for a difficult moment (a hard final set).
regression: Focus on visualizing just the first and hardest exercise of the session.

name: Competition Visualization
steps: Sit quietly in the hours or day before competition.
Picture arriving at the venue, seeing the setting in as much detail as possible.
Mentally rehearse the competition itself, including a moment of adversity and successfully working through it.
Finish by visualizing the specific feeling of having competed to your full capability, regardless of the final result.
focus: The full arc of the competition, including successfully navigating one difficult moment.
benefits: Rehearsing adversity, not just success, builds genuine resilience rather than fragile overconfidence
Widely used at elite levels of sport as a core, evidence-informed preparation tool
Anchoring success to effort and execution (not just outcome) protects confidence regardless of the result
science: Elite sport psychology research consistently supports imagery rehearsal, including rehearsal of setbacks, as improving competitive readiness and emotional regulation.
mistakes: Only visualizing a perfect, flawless outcome, which leaves no mental preparation for real setbacks that occur.
Tying the entire visualization to winning rather than to controllable process and effort.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Add a second adversity scenario (a bad start, a mistake) and rehearse the recovery from each.
regression: Focus only on the first few minutes of the competition.

name: Student Focus Reset
steps: Sit at the study desk, spine tall, and close the eyes.
Picture yourself studying calmly, understanding the material clearly as you go.
Extend the image into an exam scenario — reading a question calmly, recalling the answer with ease.
Notice the feeling of quiet confidence this creates, and carry it into the actual study session.
focus: A calm, capable mental image of studying and recalling information with ease.
benefits: Rehearsing calm competence directly counters the common pattern of exam-related catastrophic thinking
Short enough to use immediately before any study block or exam
Builds a specific, positive association with the studying process itself
science: Visualization paired with calming breathwork is used in educational psychology interventions to reduce test anxiety and improve perceived academic self-efficacy.
mistakes: Letting the visualization drift into worry about failing instead of picturing calm, capable performance.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend to visualizing a full exam from start to finish, including recovering from one hard question.
regression: Shorten to visualizing just the first five calm minutes of the study session.

name: Office Reset
steps: Sit at the desk, close the eyes or lower the gaze, and take one long exhale.
Mentally set aside the last task, picturing it being placed in a drawer for now.
Relax the shoulders down and away from the ears, softening the jaw and hands.
Take a few slow breaths, then open the eyes ready for what's next.
focus: The physical release of tension in the shoulders, jaw, and hands.
benefits: A genuinely realistic length for use between back-to-back meetings or tasks
The mental 'setting aside' image helps create psychological separation between tasks
Regular micro-resets are associated with sustained afternoon focus and reduced end-of-day fatigue
science: Brief workplace mindfulness breaks are associated in occupational research with reduced perceived stress and improved task-switching.
mistakes: Skipping this because it feels 'too short to matter' — brief, frequent resets are the entire design intent.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Pair with the Two-Minute Desk Reset Breath for a fuller reset between demanding meetings.
regression: Reduce to a single slow exhale and shoulder release if time is extremely limited.

name: Music Meditation
steps: Choose one calming instrumental piece of music without lyrics.
Sit comfortably and close the eyes, letting the music play.
Rest attention on a single element of the music — the melody, a repeated rhythm, or one instrument.
Whenever a thought pulls attention away, gently return it to that chosen element of the sound.
focus: One chosen element of the music (melody, rhythm, or single instrument).
benefits: Using an external, ever-changing anchor (music) is often easier for beginners than the more subtle sensation of breath
Removes the awkwardness some people feel with silent meditation
Naturally adaptable — any calming instrumental track can be used
science: Music-assisted attention practices are used as an accessible entry point to meditation, particularly for people who find silent practice difficult to sustain.
mistakes: Letting the mind drift into passive listening rather than actively choosing one element to focus on.
Choosing music with lyrics, which pulls attention toward language and story instead of pure sound.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Switch the focal element (melody to rhythm) partway through for a more dynamic practice.
regression: Simply listen without a specific focal element if the added structure feels distracting.

name: Rain Meditation
steps: Sit or lie comfortably and close the eyes.
Imagine sitting near a window, watching gentle rain fall outside.
Picture the rhythm of the raindrops, and the distant, soft rumble of far-off thunder.
Let the imagined sound of the rain become a steady backdrop for slow, calm breathing.
focus: The imagined rhythmic sound of rainfall.
benefits: Rhythmic natural sounds, even imagined, are a well-known and broadly effective relaxation cue
The steady 'white noise' quality of rain imagery makes it easier to sustain attention than more complex scenes
science: Rhythmic ambient sound, including rainfall, is commonly used in clinical and consumer relaxation tools due to its consistent calming association.
mistakes: Letting the scene shift into worry about actual weather or travel plans instead of staying with the calming imagery.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend into a full pre-sleep practice by continuing the imagery until sleep arrives.
regression: Focus on just the sound without building the full visual window scene.

name: Campfire Meditation
steps: Sit comfortably and close the eyes.
Imagine sitting beside a warm, gently crackling campfire.
Notice the imagined warmth on the skin and the sound of the wood crackling.
Let attention rest on the fire's imagined movement, returning to it whenever thoughts pull away.
focus: The imagined warmth and crackling sound of a campfire.
benefits: Fire-gazing is a naturally absorbing, ancient form of attention rest that many people find easier than silent stillness
The combined warmth and sound imagery gives attention two anchors to return to
science: Naturalistic, absorbing visual and auditory imagery is used in relaxation training as an accessible substitute for real-world restorative environments.
mistakes: Trying to conjure a perfectly vivid image — a general impression of warmth and sound is sufficient.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Add the imagined scent of woodsmoke for a fuller sensory scene.
regression: Focus on just the sound of crackling wood.

name: Walking Meditation
steps: Choose a quiet stretch of path, indoors or outdoors, at least 5-10 steps long.
Walk slowly, bringing full attention to the sensation of each foot lifting, moving, and landing.
When you reach the end of the path, pause, turn, and continue, keeping the same slow attention.
Whenever the mind wanders to a plan or worry, gently return attention to the feeling of the feet.
focus: The physical sensation of each footstep — lifting, moving, landing.
benefits: Combines gentle physical movement with attention training, useful for people who find seated stillness difficult
A practical option for a study or work break that also involves standing up and moving
Can be practiced almost anywhere with a few metres of clear space
science: Walking meditation is a traditional mindfulness practice with modern evidence supporting its use as an accessible alternative to seated meditation for improving present-moment attention.
mistakes: Walking at a normal, fast pace instead of deliberately slowing down.
Using the walk to plan the day instead of attending to the sensation of walking.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend the path length and duration for a longer walking practice.
regression: Practice in place, lifting the feet in small steps if space is very limited.

name: Tea Meditation
steps: Prepare a cup of tea (or any warm beverage) and sit down without other distractions.
Before drinking, notice the warmth of the cup in the hands and the rising steam.
Take the first sip slowly, noticing the temperature, taste, and sensation fully.
Continue drinking slowly, returning attention to taste and warmth each time it drifts.
focus: The taste, warmth, and physical sensation of drinking the beverage.
benefits: An easy entry point to mindfulness for people who find abstract meditation instructions difficult
Turns an already-existing daily habit into a genuine practice, requiring no extra time
Builds the general skill of single-tasking, which transfers to other daily activities
science: Everyday-activity mindfulness (eating or drinking meditations) is a well-established technique for building present-moment awareness in a low-barrier, practical way.
mistakes: Drinking while scrolling a phone or watching a screen — the whole point is undivided attention.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Extend the practice to the whole process of preparing the tea, not just drinking it.
regression: Practice for just the first sip if a full cup of undivided attention feels difficult at first.

name: Desk Neck and Shoulder Reset
breathing: Slow breathing paired with gentle movement
steps: Sit tall and close the eyes or lower the gaze.
Slowly roll the shoulders back and down three times, breathing out on each roll.
Gently tilt the head side to side, noticing any tension without forcing a stretch.
Finish with three slow breaths, mentally releasing the accumulated tension of the last work block.
focus: Physical sensation of tension release in the neck and shoulders.
benefits: Combines light physical movement with a brief mental reset, addressing both the mental and postural cost of desk work
Short enough for genuine, repeated daily use between meetings
science: Combining brief movement with mindful attention is supported in occupational health research as an effective, low-barrier intervention for desk-based stress and musculoskeletal tension.
mistakes: Rushing through the shoulder rolls mechanically instead of pairing them with attention and breath.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Add the Band Pull-Apart exercise immediately after for a fuller physical-mental reset.
regression: Perform seated with eyes open if closing them is not practical in the workplace.

name: Muscle Gain Focus: Performance and Recovery
steps: Sit comfortably and bring to mind the specific training goal for this phase — strength or size.
Visualize a recent session where effort and form both felt strong, recalling that feeling in the body.
Extend the image forward to recovery — adequate sleep, food, and rest supporting that effort.
Let a felt sense of patient, consistent capability settle before returning to daily activity.
focus: The felt sense of strong effort paired with the image of adequate recovery supporting it.
benefits: Explicitly linking training visualization to recovery habits reinforces that gains happen outside the gym as much as in it
Reduces the common trap of visualizing only the workout while neglecting sleep, food, and rest as part of the process
science: Goal visualization that includes the full behaviour chain (effort plus recovery) is more strongly associated with sustained adherence than visualization of the outcome alone.
mistakes: Visualizing only the physique outcome without the process of training and recovering that gets there.
tips: Thoughts will keep arising throughout this practice — that is normal and expected, not a sign of failure. The skill is not stopping thought, but noticing when attention has drifted, accepting the thought without judgment, letting it pass, and gently returning to the chosen focus. Repeating this return, again and again, is the practice itself.
progression: Pair with a written note of tonight's specific recovery action (sleep time, a meal, a stretch).
regression: Focus only on the training-effort portion of the visualization.

name: Asthma
overview: A condition involving airway sensitivity that can cause breathlessness, wheezing, or chest tightness, particularly during exertion or in cold, dry, or pollen-heavy air. Well-managed asthma is compatible with regular exercise, and consistent aerobic activity is generally associated with improved lung function and reduced symptom frequency over time. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Always warm up gradually for at least 10 minutes before higher-intensity work.
Keep any prescribed reliever medication accessible during every session.
Favour warm, humid environments over cold, dry air where possible.
Build intensity progressively across weeks rather than jumping straight to high-intensity intervals.
recommended: Swimming in a warm, humidified pool environment
Cycling at a controlled, steady intensity
Yoga with an emphasis on breathing control
avoid_ex: Sudden maximal-effort sprints without a warm-up
Exercise in cold, dry outdoor air during flare-prone seasons
High-pollen outdoor exercise during personal trigger seasons
yoga: Box breathing (between exercise bouts, not during acute breathlessness)
breathing: Diaphragmatic breathing as a daily practice
stretch: Standing quadriceps and hamstring stretches post-session (avoid stretches that restrict chest expansion)
intensity: Moderate, building gradually; avoid sudden jumps in intensity or duration.
recovery: A gradual, structured warm-up and cool-down are especially important; symptom diaries can help identify personal triggers.
red_flags: Chest tightness or wheezing that does not resolve with rest and reliever use
Bluish lips or fingertips
Severe breathlessness preventing speech — this requires emergency care

name: High Cholesterol
overview: Elevated blood lipid levels are a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor. Regular aerobic exercise, combined with resistance training, is consistently associated with improved lipid profiles, particularly increases in protective HDL cholesterol. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Aim for consistent aerobic activity most days of the week, alongside 2-3 resistance sessions.
Favour activities that can be sustained long-term over short, unsustainable intensity spikes.
Combine exercise guidance with the dietary and medical guidance of a qualified professional.
recommended: Jump rope (once cardiovascular clearance is confirmed)
avoid_ex: Extremely high-intensity efforts without any cardiovascular clearance if other risk factors are present
breathing: General wellbeing meditation (Section 8) for stress reduction, which indirectly supports cardiovascular health
stretch: Standing lower back and hamstring stretches post-session
intensity: Moderate to vigorous, built up gradually with medical clearance if other cardiovascular risk factors coexist.
recovery: This is a long-term, consistency-driven goal; abrupt intensity spikes offer little added benefit over steady, sustained activity.
red_flags: Chest pain, pressure, or unusual shortness of breath during exercise (stop immediately and seek care)

name: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)
overview: Persistently elevated blood pressure increases cardiovascular strain over time. Regular moderate aerobic exercise is one of the most consistently evidenced non-pharmacological tools for lowering blood pressure, though exercise selection should avoid movements that spike pressure acutely and dangerously. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Favour rhythmic, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise over near-maximal effort.
Breathe continuously through all resistance exercises — never hold the breath under load (the Valsalva manoeuvre can spike pressure sharply).
Monitor for dizziness or headache during exercise and stop if either occurs.
Build intensity gradually and avoid abrupt, unaccustomed maximal efforts.
recommended: Light-to-moderate resistance training with continuous breathing
Yoga emphasising breath and gentle movement
avoid_ex: Heavy near-maximal lifting (1-3 rep max attempts)
Breath-holding during any resistance exercise
Extended isometric holds at high effort (e.g. a maximal wall sit)
Rapid, uncontrolled inversions
breathing: Grounding awareness meditation for daily stress reduction
stretch: Gentle standing stretches, avoiding any position with the head lowered below the heart for extended periods
intensity: Low to moderate, avoiding breath-holding and extreme exertion spikes.
recovery: Consistency and breath control matter more than intensity; blood pressure should be reasonably controlled before beginning vigorous training, per a physician's guidance.
red_flags: Severe headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, or extreme dizziness during exercise (seek emergency care)

name: Prediabetes
overview: A state of elevated blood glucose below the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Regular physical activity, particularly a combination of aerobic and resistance training, is one of the most effective known tools for improving insulin sensitivity and can meaningfully reduce progression risk. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Combine both aerobic and resistance training weekly — the two provide complementary metabolic benefits.
Where possible, take a short walk after meals, which can help moderate post-meal blood glucose.
Aim for consistency across most days of the week rather than concentrated, infrequent sessions.
recommended: Resistance training targeting major muscle groups
avoid_ex: Prolonged sedentary stretches with no movement breaks (the modification here is behavioural — build in movement — rather than avoiding any specific exercise)
breathing: Motivation-focused meditation to support consistent adherence
intensity: Moderate, consistent activity most days; resistance training at least twice weekly.
recovery: This is a genuinely modifiable state with strong evidence for exercise as a primary intervention; consistency matters more than any single session's intensity.
red_flags: Unusual excessive thirst, frequent urination, or unexplained fatigue (discuss with a doctor)

name: Type 2 Diabetes
overview: A metabolic condition involving impaired insulin sensitivity and elevated blood glucose. Exercise is a well-established component of management alongside medical and dietary guidance, improving glucose regulation and reducing long-term complication risk. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Coordinate exercise timing with medication and meal schedules under a doctor's guidance, particularly for anyone on insulin or medications that can cause low blood sugar.
Carry a fast-acting carbohydrate source during sessions in case of low blood sugar symptoms.
Check blood glucose before and after exercise if advised to do so by a healthcare provider.
Inspect the feet regularly and wear well-fitting footwear, particularly relevant given circulation and nerve-sensitivity considerations.
avoid_ex: Exercising during a period of very high or very low blood glucose without following medical guidance
High-intensity exercise without prior clearance if complications such as retinopathy or neuropathy are present
stretch: General full-body stretching, avoiding excessive pressure on any areas of reduced foot sensation
intensity: Moderate, individualised, and ideally coordinated with a healthcare provider's guidance on medication timing.
recovery: Exercise is one pillar of a broader, medically supervised management plan; this entry addresses movement only.
red_flags: Symptoms of low blood sugar (shakiness, confusion, sweating) during or after exercise
Any new numbness, wounds, or infections on the feet

name: PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)
overview: A hormonal condition affecting ovulation, metabolism, and androgen levels, often associated with insulin resistance. Regular exercise, particularly resistance training combined with moderate aerobic activity, is associated with improved insulin sensitivity and menstrual regularity in many individuals. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Prioritise resistance training, which is particularly supportive for the insulin-resistance component often present.
Balance intensity with adequate recovery — chronic excessive high-intensity training can worsen hormonal stress in some individuals.
Track energy and cycle changes over time and discuss patterns with a doctor.
recommended: Yoga, particularly hip-opening and restorative sequences
avoid_ex: Chronic excessive high-intensity training without adequate recovery, which can be counterproductive for some individuals with PCOS
yoga: Bhramari (Humming Bee Breath) for stress reduction
breathing: Gratitude and emotional balance meditation; stress-reduction practices generally
intensity: Moderate, balanced with genuine recovery; avoid chronic overtraining.
recovery: Hormonal response to exercise varies significantly between individuals; adjust based on energy, sleep, and cycle feedback over time, in partnership with a healthcare provider.
red_flags: Severe pelvic pain
Very heavy or prolonged bleeding
Signs of significant hormonal imbalance requiring medical evaluation

name: Hypothyroidism
overview: An underactive thyroid can slow metabolism and contribute to fatigue, weight gain, and reduced exercise tolerance. With appropriate medical management, regular moderate exercise supports energy levels, metabolic health, and mood. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Expect exercise tolerance to improve as thyroid levels are medically stabilised — be patient with early fatigue.
Favour consistency over intensity, especially in the early stages of treatment.
Prioritise adequate sleep and recovery, as fatigue can be more pronounced with this condition.
avoid_ex: Pushing through severe unaccustomed fatigue to 'match' a pre-diagnosis training intensity
intensity: Low to moderate initially, progressing as energy levels and medical management improve.
recovery: Exercise tolerance often improves meaningfully once thyroid hormone levels are medically stabilised; coordinate expectations with a treating physician.
red_flags: Unusual chest discomfort, palpitations, or extreme fatigue disproportionate to effort

name: Hyperthyroidism
overview: An overactive thyroid can increase heart rate, metabolism, and anxiety, and may cause muscle weakness or tremor. Exercise guidance depends heavily on whether the condition is medically controlled, and intensity should generally be conservative until levels are stabilised. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Avoid high-intensity or high-heart-rate training until the condition is medically stabilised, given the baseline elevated heart rate and cardiovascular strain.
Monitor for palpitations, tremor, or unusual heat intolerance during exercise.
Prioritise gentle, restorative movement while working with a physician on medical management.
recommended: Swimming at an easy pace, once cleared by a physician
avoid_ex: High-intensity interval training
Heavy resistance training
Any vigorous cardiovascular exercise until medically cleared
Hot yoga or exercise in high heat (heat intolerance is common)
breathing: Grounding awareness meditation for associated anxiety symptoms
stretch: Gentle stretching only, avoiding intense or prolonged holds
intensity: Low, and only progressed with explicit medical clearance as levels stabilise.
recovery: This condition carries genuine cardiovascular considerations at rest; exercise intensity decisions should be made in direct consultation with a treating physician.
red_flags: Rapid or irregular heartbeat
Chest pain
Significant tremor or heat intolerance during activity

name: Obesity
overview: A condition involving excess body fat that can increase risk for several other chronic conditions. Regular physical activity supports weight management, cardiovascular health, and mobility, and benefits accrue even without dramatic weight change. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Begin with low-impact activities to protect the joints while building an activity habit.
Progress duration before intensity in the early weeks.
Pair exercise with professional dietary guidance for weight-related goals — exercise alone has a modest direct effect on weight compared to combined approaches.
Celebrate non-scale progress markers such as improved stamina, strength, and mobility.
avoid_ex: High-impact plyometrics (box jumps, jump squats) before joint conditioning is established
Extended running before a walking base is built
stretch: Gentle full-body stretching, seated variations where floor-based stretches are uncomfortable
intensity: Low to moderate initially, building duration before intensity.
recovery: Sustainable, joint-friendly progression produces better long-term adherence than an aggressive early approach; small consistent sessions compound significantly over months.
red_flags: Chest pain, severe joint pain, or breathlessness disproportionate to effort

name: Arthritis
overview: A group of conditions involving joint inflammation, pain, and stiffness. Contrary to the instinct to rest completely, regular gentle movement is generally associated with reduced pain and improved joint function over time, though exercise selection should respect flare-ups. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Favour low-impact movement that keeps joints moving without heavy impact loading.
Warm up thoroughly — arthritic joints often respond well to a longer, gentler warm-up.
Scale back intensity, not eliminate movement entirely, during flare-up periods.
Work within a pain-free or mildly-uncomfortable range rather than pushing through sharp pain.
recommended: Swimming and water aerobics (minimal joint loading)
Gentle resistance training with controlled range of motion
avoid_ex: High-impact activities during a flare (running, jumping, heavy loaded squats)
Forcing a joint through a painful range purely to 'complete' a prescribed exercise
stretch: Gentle joint-specific mobility work (see Mobility Library) rather than aggressive static stretching
intensity: Low to moderate, adjusted flexibly around flare-ups.
recovery: Movement is generally protective for joint health when appropriately dosed; working with a physiotherapist for individualised joint-specific guidance is recommended.
red_flags: Sudden joint swelling, redness, or warmth (possible acute flare requiring medical review)
Sharp pain that persists after stopping activity

name: Lower Back Pain (Non-Specific, Chronic)
overview: Persistent lower back discomfort without a specific identified structural cause. Contrary to historical advice to rest completely, graded return to movement — particularly building core and hip strength — is now the generally preferred approach for most non-specific chronic lower back pain. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Begin with gentle, pain-tolerant movement rather than complete rest, which can worsen deconditioning over time.
Build core and hip strength progressively — a stronger surrounding musculature generally supports the spine.
Avoid any single movement that consistently and sharply worsens symptoms, and progress around it.
Work with a physiotherapist for an individualised diagnosis and plan where pain is persistent or severe.
avoid_ex: Heavy spinal loading (deadlifts, loaded good mornings) before a rehabilitation foundation is built
Prolonged bed rest, which is generally not recommended for non-specific back pain
breathing: Body scan relaxation for pain-related tension
stretch: Knee-to-chest stretches within a comfortable range
intensity: Low initially, building gradually as tolerance and confidence improve.
recovery: A graded return to activity, guided by a physiotherapist, is generally preferred over prolonged rest for non-specific chronic lower back pain.
red_flags: Pain with numbness, tingling, or weakness radiating down a leg
Loss of bladder or bowel control (seek emergency care immediately)
Pain following significant trauma

name: Neck Pain (Chronic, Postural)
overview: Persistent neck discomfort often associated with prolonged forward-head posture, such as extended desk or phone use. Targeted postural strengthening and mobility work, combined with ergonomic adjustment, generally improve symptoms over time. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Address workstation ergonomics alongside any exercise plan — screen height and posture matter significantly.
Build deep neck flexor and upper back strength rather than relying on stretching alone.
Take regular movement breaks during prolonged desk work.
Progress gently — the neck responds well to light, frequent movement rather than infrequent intense sessions.
avoid_ex: Aggressive neck stretching during an acute flare
Heavy overhead loading before postural strength is established
breathing: Desk Neck and Shoulder Reset meditation
intensity: Low to moderate, favouring frequent brief sessions over occasional intense ones.
recovery: Postural, ergonomic, and exercise interventions together tend to outperform any single approach alone for this presentation.
red_flags: Numbness or tingling radiating into the arm or hand
Severe pain following trauma
Pain accompanied by headache, dizziness, or visual changes

name: Osteoporosis
overview: A condition of reduced bone density that increases fracture risk. Weight-bearing and resistance exercise are among the most effective tools for supporting bone density, though certain high-risk movements should be avoided or modified. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Prioritise weight-bearing and resistance exercise, which provide the mechanical loading stimulus bones need.
Emphasise balance training to reduce fall risk, since falls are the primary mechanism of fracture.
Avoid movements involving spinal flexion combined with rotation under load (a common recommendation in osteoporosis-specific guidance).
Progress load gradually under professional guidance, particularly for anyone newly diagnosed.
recommended: Balance training (Tree Pose, single-leg stance work)
avoid_ex: High-impact activities without prior clearance if fracture risk is elevated
Loaded spinal flexion-rotation movements (e.g. a weighted sit-up with a twist)
Movements with a significant fall risk without adequate balance preparation
breathing: Confidence-building visualization to support consistent participation despite fracture-risk anxiety
stretch: Gentle standing stretches, avoiding forceful spinal flexion
intensity: Low to moderate, with a strong emphasis on progressive resistance and balance work under guidance.
recovery: Weight-bearing and resistance exercise are strongly supported for bone health; a physiotherapist or specialist can advise on individually appropriate loading given specific bone density results.
red_flags: A fall, even without immediate pain
New or worsening back pain, which can indicate a vertebral change and warrants medical review

name: Acid Reflux (GERD)
overview: A condition where stomach acid frequently flows back into the oesophagus, causing heartburn and discomfort. Exercise timing and choice of movement can meaningfully affect symptom frequency. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Avoid exercising immediately after a large meal — allow 2-3 hours where possible.
Favour upright activities over positions involving significant forward bending or inversion.
Stay well hydrated, but avoid large volumes of fluid immediately before exercise.
Notice any specific movements that reliably trigger symptoms and modify around them.
avoid_ex: Heavy forward-flexed movements on a full stomach (e.g. weighted sit-ups shortly after eating)
Inversions or deep forward folds immediately post-meal
yoga: Diaphragmatic breathing (practiced away from meal times)
breathing: General stress-relief meditation, as stress can be a symptom contributor for some individuals
stretch: Gentle standing stretches; avoid deep forward folds shortly after eating
intensity: Moderate, timed carefully around meals.
recovery: Meal timing relative to exercise is often as important as exercise selection itself for this condition.
red_flags: Difficulty swallowing
Unintended weight loss
Vomiting blood or black stool (seek urgent medical care)

name: IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome)
overview: A functional digestive condition causing abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. Moderate, consistent exercise is generally associated with symptom improvement, while very high-intensity or high-impact exercise can worsen symptoms for some individuals. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Favour moderate, consistent activity over sporadic high-intensity sessions.
Notice individual patterns — some people tolerate certain exercise types better than others; track and adjust.
Stay adequately hydrated, and be mindful of caffeine or pre-workout supplement intake, which can aggravate symptoms for some.
Manage stress alongside exercise, given the well-documented gut-brain connection in IBS.
recommended: Cycling at a moderate, steady pace
avoid_ex: Very high-intensity interval training if it reliably triggers symptoms for the individual
High-impact running immediately after eating
breathing: Stress-relief meditation, given the documented gut-brain axis relevance to IBS symptoms
stretch: Gentle abdominal-area stretches, seated spinal twists
intensity: Low to moderate, adjusted based on individual symptom response.
recovery: Individual symptom triggers vary significantly; a structured trial-and-adjust approach, ideally with a dietitian or gastroenterologist, tends to work better than a one-size-fits-all plan.
red_flags: Blood in stool
Unintended significant weight loss
Severe abdominal pain (seek medical evaluation)

name: Constipation
overview: Infrequent or difficult bowel movements. Regular physical activity is a well-supported, low-risk tool for improving bowel motility alongside adequate hydration and fibre intake. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Build in regular daily movement, even brief walks, which support bowel motility.
Combine exercise with adequate hydration and fibre intake as part of an overall approach.
Consider gentle abdominal and twisting movements, which may support digestive movement.
recommended: Yoga twists (Seated Spinal Twist, Half Lord of the Fishes)
avoid_ex: No specific major exercise avoidances for this condition beyond general safety principles
yoga: Diaphragmatic breathing, which engages the abdominal region during the breathing cycle
intensity: Low to moderate; consistency (daily movement) matters more than intensity for this goal.
recovery: Movement is a supportive tool alongside hydration and dietary fibre; persistent symptoms warrant medical evaluation.
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain
Blood in stool
Constipation alternating with diarrhoea persisting beyond a few weeks

name: Stress (Chronic)
overview: Persistent activation of the body's stress response, which can affect sleep, mood, immune function, and cardiovascular health over time. Regular physical activity is one of the most consistently evidenced tools for reducing perceived stress. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Incorporate both vigorous exercise (for acute stress discharge) and gentler practices like yoga or walking (for parasympathetic recovery).
Avoid relying solely on very high-intensity training if it is not paired with adequate recovery, which can itself become a stressor.
Build in brief daily movement rather than relying only on occasional longer sessions.
avoid_ex: Excessive, under-recovered high-intensity training used as the sole coping strategy, which can compound rather than relieve chronic stress
breathing: Stress Relief: Release and Soften meditation
intensity: Variable — both vigorous and gentle activity have a role; the key is consistency and adequate recovery.
recovery: A combined approach of movement, breathing practice, and adequate sleep tends to outperform any single intervention alone.
red_flags: Stress accompanied by persistent low mood, hopelessness, or thoughts of self-harm (seek professional mental health support)

name: Anxiety
overview: A state of persistent worry, nervousness, or unease, which can be accompanied by physical symptoms such as a racing heart or muscle tension. Regular moderate exercise is a well-supported complementary tool for reducing anxiety symptoms. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Favour rhythmic, predictable activities over unpredictable high-stimulation environments if anxiety includes a sensory-overwhelm component.
Be mindful that very high caffeine or stimulant pre-workout intake can mimic or worsen anxious physical sensations for some individuals.
Combine exercise with breathing practice for a fuller nervous-system approach.
avoid_ex: Very high-intensity, unfamiliar environments if they provoke overwhelm (introduce new formats gradually instead)
intensity: Low to moderate, prioritising consistency and a felt sense of safety in the exercise environment.
recovery: Exercise is a well-evidenced complementary tool for anxiety management, and works particularly well alongside professional support when anxiety is persistent or significantly impacts daily functioning.
red_flags: Anxiety accompanying chest pain, or a first-time panic attack with unclear cause (seek medical evaluation to rule out other causes)
Anxiety significantly impacting daily functioning (seek professional mental health support)

name: Poor Sleep (Chronic Insomnia Pattern)
overview: Persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep. Regular daytime physical activity is associated with improved sleep quality and reduced time to fall asleep, though exercise timing relative to bedtime matters. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Exercise earlier in the day where possible — vigorous exercise very close to bedtime can be stimulating for some individuals.
Get outdoor light exposure during morning or daytime activity where possible, which supports circadian rhythm.
Use gentle, calming movement (yoga, stretching) in the evening rather than vigorous training.
Pair exercise with a consistent wind-down breathing practice before bed.
recommended: Morning or afternoon walking, cycling, or resistance training
avoid_ex: Vigorous, high-intensity training within 1-2 hours of bedtime, if it is personally found to be stimulating
intensity: Moderate during the day; low and calming in the evening hours.
recovery: The timing of activity relative to bedtime is often as important as the activity itself; individual sensitivity to evening exercise varies.
red_flags: Insomnia persisting most nights for several weeks with significant daytime impact (seek medical or sleep-specialist evaluation)

name: Sedentary Lifestyle
overview: Extended periods of low physical activity, common in desk-based work or limited-mobility living situations. Even modest increases in daily movement are associated with meaningful health benefits, and the transition from none to some activity carries the largest relative benefit of any activity increase. This entry provides general exercise-modification guidance only. It is not a diagnosis, medical advice, or a substitute for guidance from a qualified physician regarding this individual's specific case. Any new or worsening symptoms should be discussed with a doctor before continuing exercise.
guidelines: Start with small, sustainable additions — a 10-minute daily walk is a genuinely valuable starting point.
Break up prolonged sitting with brief movement every 30-60 minutes where possible.
Build consistency before intensity; a modest daily habit outperforms an ambitious plan abandoned within weeks.
Choose activities that fit realistically into the existing daily schedule and environment.
avoid_ex: Jumping directly into high-intensity or high-volume training without any base level of conditioning
stretch: Office desk-break stretching routine (see Warm-Up/Cool-Down libraries)
intensity: Low initially, focused entirely on building a consistent daily movement habit.
recovery: The single largest health benefit comes from moving from zero activity to some regular activity; perfectionism about the 'ideal' program is a common barrier worth avoiding.
red_flags: New chest pain, breathlessness, or joint pain when beginning activity after a long inactive period (seek medical clearance before starting if any pre-existing conditions are suspected)

name: Fever
overview: An elevated body temperature usually indicating the body is fighting an infection. Exercise during an active fever is generally discouraged, since it further raises core temperature and heart rate demand at a time the body's resources are already directed toward immune response. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Rest completely during the active fever period — this is one of the few situations where full rest is the right call.
Avoid all structured exercise until body temperature has been normal for at least 24 hours.
When resuming, begin with very light activity (short walks) before returning to prior training intensity.
Return to full intensity gradually over several days, roughly matching how many days were lost.
diet: Stay hydrated with water and, if appetite allows, easily digestible foods; a doctor or general practitioner can advise on specific nutrition for the underlying illness.
hydration: Increase fluid intake significantly above normal, especially if sweating.
timeline: Typically 3-7 days from fever onset, though this varies with the underlying cause; always let symptom resolution guide the timeline rather than a fixed calendar count.
resume: Resume with light walking once temperature has been normal for 24 hours; return to full training over the following week.
Do not resume high-intensity training until energy levels feel genuinely normal, not just 'better than yesterday'.
red_flags: Chest pain, difficulty breathing, confusion, or a fever that persists beyond a few days (seek medical care)
Fever with a stiff neck or severe headache (seek urgent medical care)

name: Common Cold
overview: A mild upper respiratory viral illness causing congestion, sore throat, and mild fatigue. A widely used practical guideline is the 'neck check' — symptoms above the neck (runny nose, mild sore throat) generally allow light exercise, while symptoms below the neck (chest congestion, body aches, fever) suggest rest. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: If symptoms are limited to the head (runny nose, mild congestion) without fever, light-to-moderate exercise is often well tolerated.
Reduce intensity significantly even if exercising — this is not the time for personal bests.
Stop and rest if symptoms include fever, chest congestion, or body aches.
Prioritise sleep, which supports immune recovery more than exercise does during this period.
diet: Warm fluids, honey and ginger tea, and easily digestible, nutrient-dense foods are commonly used comfort measures; a doctor can advise on any specific remedies.
hydration: Increase fluid intake, particularly warm fluids which can ease congestion and throat discomfort.
timeline: Typically 5-10 days for a standard cold.
resume: Light walking or gentle yoga is often fine with head-only symptoms.
Return to full training intensity once energy and breathing feel fully normal.
red_flags: Symptoms worsening after day 5 instead of improving
High fever developing
Chest pain or significant breathlessness

name: Cough
overview: A persistent cough can result from many causes, from a resolving viral infection to airway irritation. Exercise, particularly activities that significantly increase breathing rate, can sometimes trigger coughing fits, so pacing and environment matter during recovery. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Reduce exercise intensity if coughing fits are triggered by exertion.
Favour warm, humid environments over cold, dry air, which can aggravate airway irritation.
Allow a longer, gentler warm-up than usual to ease into increased breathing demand.
If a cough persists beyond 2-3 weeks, seek medical evaluation rather than continuing to self-manage.
diet: Warm fluids and honey (for adults and children over one year) are commonly used comfort measures.
hydration: Adequate hydration supports thinner mucus and easier clearance.
timeline: A cough following a cold can reasonably persist for 2-3 weeks even as other symptoms resolve; a cough beyond this warrants medical review.
resume: Resume light activity as soon as it does not trigger coughing fits.
Progress intensity gradually, monitoring the cough's response at each stage.
red_flags: Coughing up blood
Severe chest pain with coughing
A cough lasting more than 3 weeks
High fever accompanying the cough

name: Throat Infection
overview: Inflammation or infection of the throat, which may be viral or bacterial, causing pain, particularly with swallowing, and sometimes fever. Exercise is generally best paused until pain and any fever resolve, particularly given the risk of certain bacterial throat infections requiring specific medical treatment and rest. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Rest from structured exercise while throat pain and any fever are present.
Seek medical evaluation for a throat infection with fever, particularly to rule out conditions requiring antibiotic treatment.
Resume gently once fever has resolved and swallowing is comfortable.
Stay well hydrated even though swallowing may be uncomfortable, using small frequent sips if needed.
diet: Warm salt-water gargling (for adults) and soft, easily swallowed foods are commonly used comfort measures; a doctor should evaluate fever or significant pain.
hydration: Small, frequent sips if swallowing is painful; avoid becoming dehydrated due to reduced fluid intake.
timeline: Typically 3-7 days depending on the cause; bacterial throat infections may require a specific antibiotic course as directed by a doctor.
resume: Resume light activity once fever has resolved and pain has substantially eased.
Return to full intensity over the following several days.
red_flags: Difficulty breathing or swallowing
Drooling (in children, this can indicate a serious airway issue)
High fever
A rash accompanying the sore throat
Symptoms lasting beyond a week without improvement

name: Typhoid Recovery
overview: A bacterial infection requiring medical diagnosis and antibiotic treatment, with a recovery period that can involve significant fatigue and weight loss even after the acute infection resolves. Return to exercise should be gradual and only after specific medical clearance. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Do not resume any exercise until explicitly cleared by the treating physician, given the risk of complications during active infection.
Expect a longer-than-usual recovery period, with fatigue often persisting for several weeks after the fever resolves.
Begin with very short, gentle walks once cleared, well below pre-illness activity levels.
Progress slowly over several weeks, prioritising nutrition and sleep alongside gradual activity.
diet: Follow the treating physician's specific dietary guidance closely during and after treatment, which is an important part of typhoid management.
hydration: Follow medical guidance closely on fluid intake during and after the acute illness.
timeline: Full recovery, including energy levels, can reasonably take several weeks to a few months; this varies significantly by individual and severity.
resume: Begin only with physician clearance; start with very short walks and progress by small increments week to week.
Full return to prior training intensity should be gradual and guided by ongoing energy and strength levels, not a fixed calendar.
red_flags: Any return or worsening of fever after apparent recovery
Severe abdominal pain
This condition requires medical diagnosis and treatment — this entry addresses post-medical-clearance activity only

name: Dengue Recovery
overview: A mosquito-borne viral infection that can cause significant fatigue, joint pain, and in some cases more serious complications requiring medical monitoring. Return to exercise should be gradual and only after medical clearance, given the potential for complications and prolonged fatigue. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Do not resume exercise until specifically cleared by a physician, given the risk of complications during and shortly after acute dengue infection.
Expect prolonged fatigue and sometimes joint pain for several weeks after the acute infection resolves — this is a well-documented pattern.
Begin with very light activity such as short, gentle walks once cleared.
Progress gradually, and stop if joint pain or fatigue worsens with activity.
diet: Follow the treating physician's guidance on nutrition and hydration during recovery, which plays an important role in this illness.
hydration: Adequate hydration is a critical part of dengue management under medical guidance during the acute phase.
timeline: Fatigue can reasonably persist for several weeks to a few months after the acute infection; this varies significantly between individuals.
resume: Begin only with physician clearance; short, gentle walks are a reasonable starting point once cleared.
Progress very gradually, monitoring joint pain and fatigue at each step.
red_flags: Any bleeding, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or difficulty breathing (these can indicate serious complications requiring emergency care)
This condition requires medical diagnosis and monitoring — this entry addresses post-medical-clearance activity only

name: Food Poisoning Recovery
overview: An acute gastrointestinal illness typically causing nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and abdominal discomfort. Exercise is best paused during active symptoms, with a focus on rehydration, and can generally resume once the gastrointestinal symptoms have settled and normal eating has resumed. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Rest completely during active vomiting or diarrhoea, prioritising rehydration over any activity.
Reintroduce light activity only once solid food is being tolerated normally again.
Begin with gentle walking rather than returning directly to intense training.
Pay particular attention to hydration and electrolyte replacement given fluid losses during the illness.
diet: Follow the standard graded reintroduction of bland, easily digestible foods as tolerated; a doctor or pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration solutions if needed.
hydration: Oral rehydration solutions are commonly recommended to replace lost fluids and electrolytes; plain water alone may be insufficient after significant fluid loss.
timeline: Typically 1-3 days for mild cases; some bacterial causes may take longer and warrant specific medical treatment.
resume: Begin with light walking once solid food is tolerated normally.
Return to full training intensity over the following few days as strength and hydration normalise.
red_flags: Signs of significant dehydration (very dark urine, dizziness, minimal urination)
Blood in vomit or stool
High fever
Symptoms lasting beyond 3 days without improvement

name: COVID-19 Recovery
overview: A viral respiratory illness with a wide range of severity, from mild to more prolonged recovery courses involving fatigue. A cautious, graded return to activity is generally recommended, given documented cases of cardiac and respiratory involvement even after seemingly mild infections. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Follow current national or local health authority guidance on return-to-activity timelines, as these have been periodically updated.
Avoid resuming intense exercise while any symptoms, including mild ones, are still present.
A graded return protocol — days of light activity before progressively increasing intensity — is generally recommended over an abrupt return.
Seek medical clearance before resuming intense training if symptoms were more than mild, or if any chest symptoms occurred.
diet: General balanced nutrition supporting immune recovery; no specific diet has strong evidence of altering the course of the illness.
hydration: Maintain normal hydration; increase somewhat if fever was present.
timeline: Highly variable — mild cases may allow return to activity within 1-2 weeks, while others report prolonged fatigue over a much longer period; individual medical guidance should shape the actual timeline.
resume: Begin with short, easy walks once free of fever and acute symptoms.
Progress intensity gradually over 1-2+ weeks, monitoring heart rate response and fatigue at each stage.
Seek medical clearance, particularly cardiac screening, before resuming intense training if the illness involved more than mild symptoms.
red_flags: Chest pain, palpitations, or unusual breathlessness during or after exercise, at any point in recovery
Symptoms suggesting the illness is worsening rather than improving

name: Migraine
overview: A neurological condition causing episodes of often severe headache, sometimes with nausea, light sensitivity, or visual disturbance. Exercise during an active migraine attack is generally not advisable, though regular moderate exercise between episodes is associated with reduced migraine frequency for many individuals. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Rest in a dark, quiet environment during an active migraine attack rather than attempting exercise.
Once the acute attack has resolved, a gradual return to light activity is generally well tolerated.
Between episodes, regular moderate aerobic exercise is associated with reduced migraine frequency for many people, though intense sudden exertion can be a trigger for some.
Identify and track any personal exercise-related triggers (dehydration, skipped meals before training, extreme heat) with a headache diary.
diet: Stay well hydrated and maintain regular meal timing, as both dehydration and skipped meals are common migraine triggers for many individuals.
hydration: Consistent, adequate hydration is a commonly cited protective factor against migraine triggers.
timeline: An acute migraine attack itself typically lasts 4-72 hours; the frequency of episodes over time varies enormously between individuals.
resume: Rest during an active attack; resume light walking once symptoms have substantially eased.
Return to full training intensity gradually, being attentive to any personal exercise-related triggers.
red_flags: A first-ever severe headache, especially with fever, stiff neck, confusion, or weakness (seek emergency care to rule out other causes)
A significant change in usual migraine pattern

name: General Fatigue
overview: A state of persistent low energy that may follow illness, poor sleep, high stress, or overtraining. Exercise selection should distinguish between fatigue that will respond well to gentle activity and fatigue that signals a need for more complete rest and recovery. This entry provides general activity-modification guidance for common recovery scenarios. It is not medical advice or a diagnosis. Timelines vary significantly between individuals, and anyone with severe, worsening, or unusual symptoms should seek medical care rather than follow a generic timeline.
modification: Distinguish between everyday tiredness (often improved by light movement) and profound fatigue or exhaustion (which usually calls for rest instead).
If fatigue follows a period of intense training, consider whether it reflects overtraining and would benefit from a deload week.
Prioritise sleep quality and quantity as a foundation before adding more exercise volume.
Reintroduce activity gradually, favouring low-intensity movement over high-intensity training until energy stabilises.
diet: A balanced, adequate-calorie diet with sufficient iron, B vitamins, and overall nutrition, as several nutritional deficiencies can present as fatigue; a doctor can test for these where fatigue is persistent.
hydration: Ensure adequate daily hydration, as even mild dehydration can present as fatigue.
timeline: Fatigue related to a short-term cause (poor sleep, minor illness) often resolves within days to a couple of weeks with proper rest; persistent fatigue beyond several weeks warrants medical evaluation.
resume: Begin with gentle walking or light stretching, monitoring how energy responds over the following days.
Gradually reintroduce structured training only once baseline energy has meaningfully improved.
red_flags: Fatigue lasting more than 2-3 weeks without clear cause or improvement
Fatigue accompanied by unexplained weight loss, fever, or other systemic symptoms (seek medical evaluation)

name: General Women's Fitness
overview: A balanced, sustainable fitness foundation for women without a specific medical or goal-driven focus, covering strength, cardiovascular health, mobility, and bone density support across all life stages.
programming: 2-3 full-body resistance sessions weekly covering all major muscle groups.
2-3 moderate cardio sessions (walking, cycling, swimming) for cardiovascular health.
1-2 mobility or yoga sessions weekly for joint health and stress management.
Progress resistance training load gradually; women are frequently under-dosed on resistance training relative to what is beneficial.
avoid_ex: No universal avoidances — individualise around any personal injury history or specific conditions
notes: Resistance training does not typically cause unwanted bulk in women due to hormonal differences from men — this is one of the most common and limiting myths in women's fitness.
Bone density benefits from resistance training are particularly valuable for long-term health.

name: Women's Weight Loss
